title: A Chemistry Primer for the Origins of Life
text:
Preface
This is a book about the basic ideas of chemistry: what atoms are, how they join into molecules, how molecules are drawn, how much of a substance there is, which way a reaction runs and how fast it goes. It explains these ideas from the beginning, for readers who have never studied chemistry or who studied it long ago and have forgotten most of it.
The ideas were chosen with one destination in mind: the chemistry of life, and in particular the question of how life began. Many popular accounts of the origin of life stop at the point where the chemistry begins. This book goes the other way. It ends with the molecules from which RNA is built, and it gives the reader the tools needed to follow the research that tries to explain how those molecules first formed and came to copy themselves. The same author’s From Atoms to RNA: An Introduction to the Chemical Origins of Life tells that story in detail; a reader who has finished the present book will find it much easier to follow, although each book can be read on its own.

title: A Chemistry Primer for the Origins of Life
text:
Who this book is for
The book is written for adult readers who are curious about chemistry and the chemistry of life. No knowledge of chemistry, physics or biology is assumed. The only mathematics assumed is arithmetic: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Powers, exponentials and logarithms, which appear throughout chemistry, are introduced from the beginning in Chapter 1. Readers who already know some school chemistry can use the book selectively, and the next section describes how the chapters depend on each other.

title: A Chemistry Primer for the Origins of Life
text:
How the book is written
Every technical term is defined when it is first used and collected in the Glossary. Occasionally an everyday example is used where it shows a quantity or an effect more clearly than an abstract statement; such examples are chosen to be physically accurate, and are never a substitute for the definition. Numerical values of physical constants and properties of substances are taken from standard reference sources, which are cited.
Each chapter opens with the question it answers and ends with a list of key points and three to five self-test questions. Answers to the self-test questions are given in Appendix C.
Questions and corrections are welcome: gokyona.wahiro@gmail.com.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
The path through the book
The twelve chapters are arranged in the order in which their ideas are needed. Chapter 1 provides the mathematical tools: powers of ten, units, exponentials and logarithms. Chapters 2 to 5 describe atoms, the bonds between them, the way molecules are drawn, and the forces that act between molecules, with water as the central example. Chapters 6 to 10 describe chemical reactions quantitatively: how amounts of substance are counted, how reactions are written, where they stop (equilibrium), which direction they run (energy), and how fast they go (rates). Chapters 11 and 12 introduce the chemistry of carbon compounds and the molecules from which RNA is built.
The chapters build on each other, and a reader new to chemistry should read them in order. A reader who knows some chemistry can begin with any chapter and use the cross-references to fill gaps.

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Conventions
Quantities are given in the units of the International System (SI), with a small number of additional units that are standard in chemistry, such as the litre and the degree Celsius; all are listed in Appendix B. British spelling is used throughout. Terms printed in bold are defined at that point and appear in the Glossary (Appendix A).

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
The question of this chapter
Chemistry describes objects that are far too small to see, present in numbers far too large to count. A single drop of water, about 0.05 millilitres, contains about 1.7 × 1021 water molecules (a calculation shown in Chapter 6), and each molecule is less than a millionth of a millimetre across. The origin of life adds a third extreme: time spans of hundreds of millions of years, set against reactions that are over in a fraction of a second. This chapter asks: how can such numbers be written, compared and calculated with? It introduces the tools used for that purpose throughout chemistry: powers of ten, units, exponential change, logarithms and probabilities.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
section: 1.1 Very large and very small numbers
text:
1.1 Very large and very small numbers

Powers of ten
A power is a number multiplied by itself a given number of times. The number being multiplied is the base, and the number of times it appears is the exponent, written as a raised number. Thus 103 (“ten to the power three”) means 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000, and 25 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
Powers of ten are especially convenient, because the exponent counts the zeros: 101 = 10, 102 = 100, 106 = 1 000 000. By definition, 100 = 1.
A negative exponent means division instead of multiplication. 10−1 is 1/10 = 0.1, 10−2 is 1/100 = 0.01, and 10−6 is one millionth, 0.000 001. For a negative power of ten, the exponent counts the places by which the decimal point moves to the left of 1: 10−3 = 0.001, with the 1 in the third decimal place.


Scientific notation
In scientific notation, a number is written as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten. For example:

5 970 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 kg, the mass of the Earth, is written 5.97 × 1024 kg (NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive 2024);
0.000 000 000 052 9 m, a characteristic radius of the hydrogen atom known as the Bohr radius, is written 5.29 × 10−11 m (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.).

To convert a number into scientific notation, move the decimal point until a single non-zero digit stands in front of it, and count the moves. Moves to the left give a positive exponent; moves to the right give a negative one. In 52 900 the point moves four places to the left, giving 5.29 × 104; in 0.0072 it moves three places to the right, giving 7.2 × 10−3.
Scientific notation does two things at once. It makes very large and very small numbers short enough to read, and it separates the two pieces of information that a number carries: the leading part says how much within a factor of ten, and the exponent says how large overall.


Calculating with powers
Three rules cover almost every calculation with powers of the same base:
\[
10^a \times 10^b = 10^{a+b}, \qquad \frac{10^a}{10^b} = 10^{a-b}, \qquad \left(10^a\right)^b = 10^{a \times b}
\]
Each rule follows from counting factors of ten. For example, 103 × 102 = (10 × 10 × 10) × (10 × 10), which contains five factors of ten, so it equals 105. Numbers in scientific notation are multiplied by multiplying the leading parts and adding the exponents:
\[
(3 \times 10^{8}) \times (2 \times 10^{-3}) = 6 \times 10^{5}
\]
and divided by dividing the leading parts and subtracting the exponents:
\[
\frac{6 \times 10^{23}}{2 \times 10^{3}} = 3 \times 10^{20}
\]
Addition and subtraction do not follow these rules: 103 + 102 is 1100, not 105. To add numbers written in scientific notation, first rewrite them with the same exponent.


Orders of magnitude
The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of ten nearest to it. Two quantities that differ by a factor of about ten differ by one order of magnitude; quantities that differ by a factor of about a million differ by six. Orders of magnitude are the natural way to compare quantities that span many powers of ten, such as the abundances of the chemical elements in the Sun, or the rates of fast and slow chemical reactions.
Figure 1.1 places some lengths from atomic physics, chemistry and biology on a scale in which each step is one order of magnitude. The span from an atomic nucleus to the Earth covers about 22 orders of magnitude.






Figure 1.1: Lengths from the atomic nucleus to the Earth, on a scale in which each step is a factor of ten. Values: proton radius about 8.4 × 10−16 m; Bohr radius 5.29 × 10−11 m; carbon-carbon single bond 1.54 × 10−10 m; length of a cell of the bacterium Escherichia coli about 2 × 10−6 m (Grossman et al. 1982); mean radius of the Earth 6.371 × 106 m.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
1.2 Quantities and units

A quantity is a number times a unit
A physical quantity, such as a length, a mass or a time, is expressed as a number multiplied by a unit. In “2.5 m”, 2.5 is the number and the metre is the unit. The number alone is meaningless: 2.5 m and 2.5 km are different lengths. In calculations, units are treated like algebraic factors. They are multiplied, divided and cancelled together with the numbers, which provides a check on every result: if the units of an answer are wrong, the calculation is wrong.


The International System of Units
Science uses the International System of Units (SI). It is built on seven base units, of which five appear in this book: the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the kelvin (K) for temperature, and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. Since 20 May 2019 every base unit has been defined by fixing the numerical value of a constant of nature (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures 2019); the mole, for example, is defined through the Avogadro constant, introduced in Chapter 6.
Other units are built from the base units and are called derived units. The joule (J), the unit of energy, equals 1 kg m2 s−2; the pascal (Pa), the unit of pressure, equals 1 kg m−1 s−2. A negative exponent on a unit means “per”: m s−1 is read “metres per second”, and kJ mol−1 is “kilojoules per mole”.


Prefixes
A prefix placed before a unit multiplies it by a power of ten (Table 1.1). A kilometre is 103 m, a nanometre is 10−9 m, and a micromole is 10−6 mol.

Prefixes also apply to non-SI units. In geology, time is measured in years, written “a” (from the Latin annus), so that 4.5 billion years is written 4.5 Ga (giga-annum) and a million years as 1 Ma.


Converting units
To convert a quantity from one unit to another, multiply it by a fraction that equals 1, written so that the unwanted unit cancels. Since 1 km = 1000 m, the fraction (1000 m)/(1 km) equals 1, and
\[
3.2\ \text{km} \times \frac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} = 3200\ \text{m}
\]
The same method converts compound units. To express 72 km per hour in metres per second:
\[
72\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \times \frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 20\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}
\]


Temperature
Temperature has two scales in common scientific use. The Celsius scale (°C) was originally defined by the freezing and boiling points of water. The kelvin scale (K) measures absolute temperature: its zero, 0 K, is the lowest temperature possible, at which no further energy can be removed from a substance. A step of one kelvin is exactly the same size as a step of one degree Celsius, and the two scales are related by
\[
T/\text{K} = t/^{\circ}\text{C} + 273.15
\]
where T is the absolute temperature and t the Celsius temperature (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures 2019). Thus 25 °C, a common laboratory temperature, is 298.15 K, and 100 °C is 373.15 K. Equations that contain a temperature, such as those for reaction rates and equilibria, always require the absolute temperature in kelvin.


Significant figures
A measured value is never exact. The number of digits used to report it, its significant figures, indicates how precisely it is known. “The mean radius of the Earth is 6371 km” (four significant figures) states the value more precisely than “about 6400 km” (two). A result calculated from measured values should not be reported with more significant figures than the least precise value used. Some values are exact by definition, such as the 273.15 in the temperature conversion and the Avogadro constant; these limit nothing.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
1.3 Exponential change

Growth by a constant factor
Many processes in chemistry and biology change by a constant factor in each interval of time, rather than by a constant amount. A population of bacteria that doubles every 20 minutes has 2 times its starting number after 20 minutes, 4 times after 40 minutes, 8 times after an hour, and 2n times after n doubling times. Change of this kind is called exponential, because the elapsed time appears in the exponent.
The difference between constant-amount and constant-factor change is enormous over long times. Adding 2 in each of ten steps gives 20. Multiplying by 2 in each of ten steps gives 210 = 1024; in thirty steps, 230, more than a billion.


Decay by a constant factor
When the factor is less than 1, the quantity decreases exponentially. The most precise example in nature is radioactive decay. A radioactive nucleus has a fixed probability of decaying in each interval of time, independent of its surroundings and of how long it has already existed. As a result, in a large number of such nuclei, the same fraction decays in every equal interval. The time in which half of the nuclei decay is called the half-life, written t1/2. After one half-life, 1/2 of the original nuclei remain; after two, 1/4; after three, 1/8; and after n half-lives,
\[
\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/t_{1/2}}
\]
where N0 is the number of nuclei at the start, N the number remaining after time t, and n = t/t1/2 the number of half-lives that have passed. Carbon-14, for example, has a half-life of 5700 years (Chechev and Bé 2012): after 11 400 years a quarter of it remains. Figure 1.2 compares exponential growth and decay.






Figure 1.2: Exponential change. Left: a quantity that doubles in each time step (orange) compared with one that grows by the same amount, the starting value, in each step (grey). Right: exponential decay, in which half of what remains is lost in each half-life; the dots mark 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16.



Exponential decay is not limited to nuclei. Whenever each molecule of a substance has the same probability of being destroyed in each second, independently of the others, the amount of substance decreases exponentially. The breakdown of sugars in water, the reaction of many molecules with water (hydrolysis, Chapter 7), and the loss of RNA strands in any natural setting all follow this pattern, at least approximately.


The number e
Exponential change can be written with any base. Doubling uses base 2 and halving uses base 1/2. In science, however, one base is used far more than any other: the number e, equal to 2.718 28… (its digits continue without repeating). It arises naturally whenever a quantity changes at a rate proportional to its own size. If a quantity grows continuously at a rate of k per unit time, measured as a fraction of its current value, then after time t it has grown by the factor
\[
e^{kt}
\]
and if it decays continuously at a fractional rate k, the fraction remaining is e−kt. Here k is called a rate constant; it has units of inverse time, for example s−1, so that the product kt has no units. The expression ex is often written exp(x), which is easier to read when x is a long expression; both forms are common.
The connection with half-lives is direct. Exponential decay written as e−kt and as (1/2)t/t½ describes the same curve, provided that
\[
t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \approx \frac{0.693}{k}
\]
The symbol ln, the natural logarithm, is explained in the next section. For now it is enough to note that a large rate constant means a short half-life, and that the two are inversely proportional: doubling k halves t1/2.


Everyday example: compound interest
Compound interest follows the same mathematics. A deposit that earns 5 % interest per year, added to the balance once a year, is multiplied by 1.05 each year. After 14 years it has grown by the factor 1.0514 = 1.98, so it has almost doubled; after 28 years by 1.0528 = 3.92, almost quadrupled. The doubling time is constant, as for any exponential growth, and is 14.2 years. The formula above, with k = 0.05 per year, gives 0.693/0.05 = 13.9 years; the small difference arises because the formula assumes that interest is added continuously rather than once a year.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
1.4 Logarithms

The logarithm answers “which power?”
The logarithm to base 10 of a number x, written log10 x, is the power to which 10 must be raised to give x. Thus log10 1000 = 3, because 103 = 1000; log10 0.01 = −2, because 10−2 = 0.01; and log10 1 = 0. Logarithms of numbers that are not exact powers of ten lie between whole numbers: log10 2 = 0.301 (to three decimal places), because 100.301 = 2.00, and log10 50 = 1.699. The logarithm of zero or of a negative number is not defined, since no power of ten is zero or negative.
A logarithm is therefore the exponent of a number written as a power of ten. It discards the leading part and keeps the order of magnitude, refined to a decimal.


Rules for logarithms
The rules for powers translate directly into rules for logarithms:
\[
\log_{10}(a \times b) = \log_{10} a + \log_{10} b, \qquad
\log_{10}\frac{a}{b} = \log_{10} a - \log_{10} b, \qquad
\log_{10}\left(a^{n}\right) = n \log_{10} a
\]
The first rule is the reason logarithms were invented: it turns multiplication into addition. It also explains a property of every logarithmic quantity: multiplying a quantity by 10 adds exactly 1 to its logarithm, and multiplying it by 2 adds 0.301.


Logarithmic scales
A logarithmic scale reports a quantity by its logarithm instead of by the quantity itself. Equal steps on such a scale correspond to equal factors, not equal amounts. Two logarithmic scales will be used in this book and are common in the chemistry of life.

The pH scale (Chapter 8) reports the acidity of a solution. The pH is minus the logarithm to base 10 of the concentration of hydrogen ions, so a solution of pH 4 contains ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration of a solution of pH 5, and a thousand times that of a solution of pH 7.
The log epsilon scale used by astronomers reports the abundance of an element in the Sun or a star. It is defined so that hydrogen has the value 12, and every step of 1 means a factor of ten fewer atoms.

Graphs can also be drawn with logarithmic axes. On a logarithmic axis, the marks 1, 10, 100 and 1000 are equally spaced. Such an axis can show, on one graph, values that differ by many orders of magnitude, and it turns exponential change into a straight line. Figure 1.3 shows the same exponential decay plotted on an ordinary (linear) axis and on a logarithmic axis.






Figure 1.3: The same exponential decay, with a half-life of 1 time unit, plotted against a linear vertical axis (left) and a logarithmic vertical axis (right). On the logarithmic axis, equal vertical steps are equal factors, and the exponential curve becomes a straight line.





The natural logarithm
Logarithms can be taken to any base. The logarithm to base e is called the natural logarithm and is written ln. Thus ln x is the power to which e must be raised to give x: ln e = 1, ln 1 = 0, and ln 2 = 0.693 (to three decimal places). The natural logarithm undoes the exponential function: ln(ex) = x and e^ln x^ = x. It obeys the same rules as log10.
Natural and base-10 logarithms differ only by a constant factor:
\[
\ln x = 2.303 \times \log_{10} x
\]
where 2.303 is ln 10, rounded to three decimal places. This factor appears whenever a natural logarithm, which arises in physical equations, is converted into a pH or another base-10 scale.
The natural logarithm explains the formula for the half-life given in the previous section. After one half-life the fraction remaining is 1/2, so e−kt½ = 1/2. Taking natural logarithms of both sides gives −k t1/2 = ln(1/2) = −ln 2, and therefore t1/2 = ln 2 / k.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
1.5 Probability

Probabilities as numbers between 0 and 1
A probability is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses how likely an event is: 0 means that it never happens, and 1 that it always happens. A probability can also be written as a percentage, so that a probability of 0.25 is 25 %. If an event has probability p, the probability that it does not happen is 1 − p.
Probabilities in chemistry usually describe the behaviour of many identical particles. When a nucleotide is added to a growing RNA chain with a probability of 0.99 of being the correct one, it means that, over many additions, 99 % are correct and 1 % are errors.


Independent events multiply
Two events are independent if the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other. The probability that two independent events both happen is the product of their probabilities. If each of n independent events has probability p, the probability that all n happen is pn.
This rule has a striking consequence for long sequences of steps. Suppose that each nucleotide added to an RNA chain is correct with probability 0.99. The probability that a chain of 100 nucleotides is copied with no error at all is
\[
0.99^{100} = 0.366
\]
so almost two-thirds of the copies contain at least one error. For a chain of 1000 nucleotides the probability falls to 0.991000 = 4.3 × 10−5, about 1 in 23 000. Figure 1.4 plots this probability for several error rates. The same calculation lies behind the idea of an error threshold in the study of the origin of life: there is a maximum length of a genetic molecule that can be copied faithfully enough to keep its information from one generation to the next.






Figure 1.4: Probability that a chain of n nucleotides is copied without error, when each nucleotide is copied correctly with probability 1 − p, for error rates p of 0.1 %, 1 % and 10 % per nucleotide. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.





Counting possibilities
When each of n positions can be filled independently with one of m possibilities, the number of different arrangements is mn. A sequence of RNA uses four different building blocks, so the number of different RNA sequences of length n is 4n. For n = 10 this is 1 048 576, about 106; for n = 40 it is about 1.2 × 1024. The set of all possible sequences of a given length is called sequence space, and its size explains why no experiment can test more than a tiny fraction of the possible RNA molecules of even moderate length.
Large counts of this kind are easiest to handle with logarithms. Since log10(4n) = n × log10 4 = 0.602 n, the number of sequences of length 40 has 0.602 × 40 = 24.1 as its logarithm, so it is about 1024.1, or 1.2 × 1024.

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
1.6 Reading graphs

Axes, variables and slope
A graph shows how one quantity depends on another. The quantity that is varied or controlled, such as time or temperature, is usually placed on the horizontal axis; the quantity that is measured is placed on the vertical axis. Each axis is labelled with the name of the quantity and its unit, often written in the form “Time (s)” or “Time / s”; the second form means that the numbers on the axis are the time divided by the unit, which are pure numbers.
The slope of a straight line is the change in the vertical quantity divided by the corresponding change in the horizontal quantity. Its unit is the vertical unit divided by the horizontal unit. On a graph of the amount of a product against time, the slope is the rate at which the product is formed. When the graph is curved, the slope at a point is the slope of the straight line that just touches the curve there.


Graphs with logarithmic axes
When one or both axes are logarithmic, as in Figure 1.3 and Figure 1.4, the meaning of position changes. Equal distances along a logarithmic axis are equal factors, so a point halfway between the marks 10 and 100 stands for about 32 (since 101.5 = 31.6), not 55. Before reading values from any scientific graph, check the labels of both axes and whether each is linear or logarithmic.
Two kinds of logarithmic graph are especially useful in chemistry. A graph of the logarithm of a quantity against time is a straight line when the quantity changes exponentially; its slope gives the rate constant. A graph of the logarithm of a rate constant against the reciprocal of the absolute temperature, 1/T, is a straight line for most chemical reactions; it is called an Arrhenius plot, and its slope gives the energy barrier of the reaction (Chapter 10).

title: 1  Numbers for Chemistry
text:
Key points

In scientific notation a number is written as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, such as 5.29 × 10−11 m. Powers multiply by adding exponents and divide by subtracting them.
A quantity is a number times a unit. SI base units used here are m, kg, s, K and mol; prefixes such as k (103), \(\mu\) (10−6) and n (10−9) multiply them by powers of ten. Units cancel like algebraic factors.
Absolute temperature T in kelvin equals the Celsius temperature plus 273.15.
Exponential change multiplies a quantity by a constant factor in each interval. Exponential decay has a constant half-life; after n half-lives a fraction (1/2)n remains.
Continuous exponential decay is written e−kt, where e = 2.718 28… and k is the rate constant; the half-life is t1/2 = ln 2 / k \(\approx\) 0.693/k.
The logarithm log10 x is the power of ten that gives x. Multiplying x by 10 adds 1 to its logarithm. The pH scale and the log epsilon scale of abundances are logarithmic.
The natural logarithm ln x is the power of e that gives x; ln x = 2.303 log10 x.
The probability that n independent events, each of probability p, all occur is pn. The number of RNA sequences of length n is 4n.
On a logarithmic axis equal distances are equal factors; exponential change appears as a straight line.

title: 2  What Matter Is Made Of
text:
The question of this chapter
Water, air, rock and living tissue look and behave nothing alike, yet all of them are built from the same small set of ingredients. This chapter asks: what are those ingredients, and how are they told apart? It distinguishes elements, compounds and mixtures, describes the three particles of which every atom is made, explains how isotopes and ions arise, and introduces the periodic table and the scale on which the masses of atoms are measured.
crumbs: 2  What Matter Is Made Of

title: 2  What Matter Is Made Of
text:
2.1 Substances and mixtures

Pure substances
A pure substance is a sample of matter with a fixed composition and fixed properties. Pure water, for example, always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same proportion by mass, and at a pressure of one standard atmosphere it always freezes at 0 °C and boils close to 100 °C. A mixture contains two or more pure substances whose proportions can vary. Sea water, air and granite are mixtures: their compositions differ from place to place, and their components can be separated by physical means such as evaporation, distillation or sorting, without any chemical change.


Elements and compounds
Pure substances are of two kinds. An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by any chemical process. Hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, iron and gold are elements. A compound is a pure substance made of two or more elements combined in fixed proportions. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen; table salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine. A compound can be broken down into its elements by chemical reactions, and its properties are usually quite different from those of the elements it contains: sodium is a soft, reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous green gas, but sodium chloride is the salt sprinkled on food.
Figure 2.1 summarises these categories.






Figure 2.1: Classification of matter. A mixture can be separated into pure substances by physical means; a compound can be separated into elements only by chemical reactions; an element cannot be broken down further by chemical means.





Atoms and molecules
Every element consists of tiny particles called atoms. An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity. All atoms of one element behave chemically in the same way, and differ from the atoms of every other element.
In most compounds, atoms are held together in groups called molecules. A molecule is a group of two or more atoms bonded together, and it is the smallest unit of a compound that has the compound’s chemical identity. A molecule of water consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Some elements also exist as molecules: the oxygen in air consists of molecules containing two oxygen atoms each, and the nitrogen of air likewise of two-atom molecules. Not every compound is made of separate molecules; sodium chloride, for example, is a continuous arrangement of charged particles, described in Section 2.4.


Chemical formulas
A chemical formula states which elements a substance contains, using one- or two-letter element symbols, and how many atoms of each are present, using subscript numbers. The formula of water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms (H) and one oxygen atom (O); a subscript of 1 is not written. Oxygen gas is O2, carbon dioxide is CO2, and methane, the main component of natural gas, is CH4. Some symbols come from Latin names: sodium is Na (natrium) and potassium is K (kalium). A formula of this kind gives the composition of a molecule but not the arrangement of its atoms; Chapter 4 describes how that arrangement is drawn.


Solid, liquid and gas
The same substance can exist as a solid, a liquid or a gas, depending on temperature and pressure. These are the three common states of matter, and they differ in how the particles are arranged and how freely they move.

In a solid, the particles are packed closely and held in fixed positions, about which they vibrate. A solid keeps its own shape.
In a liquid, the particles are still close together but can move past one another. A liquid takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume.
In a gas, the particles are far apart compared with their own size and move freely in all directions. A gas fills any container it is placed in.

A change from one state to another, such as melting or boiling, does not change the molecules themselves: ice, liquid water and steam all consist of H2O molecules. What changes is the strength of the attraction between molecules compared with the energy of their motion. These attractions between molecules are the subject of Chapter 5.

text:
2.2 Inside the atom

Three particles
An atom consists of a small, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by a much larger region occupied by electrons (Figure 2.2). The nucleus contains two kinds of particle: protons, which carry a positive electric charge, and neutrons, which carry no charge. Protons and neutrons are known together as nucleons.
Electric charge is measured in coulombs (C). The charge of a proton is +e and that of an electron is −e, where e, the elementary charge, is exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 C (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). No smaller charge has ever been observed on a free particle, so the charge of any atom or molecule is a whole-number multiple of e.
Table 2.1 compares the three particles. The proton and the neutron have almost the same mass, while the electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). As a result, more than 99.9 % of the mass of an atom resides in its nucleus.

Mostly empty space
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom. An atom has a radius of 1 to 2 × 10−10 m, whereas a nucleus ranges from about 4 × 10−15 m across for carbon to about 15 × 10−15 m for lead (Encyclopaedia Britannica, n.d.). The atom is therefore tens of thousands of times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus of a carbon atom were enlarged to the size of a pea, about 5 mm across, the atom would be several hundred metres across, while still containing almost all of its mass in the pea.
The electrons do not circle the nucleus along fixed paths like planets. Quantum mechanics, the physical theory of matter on the atomic scale, describes each electron by the probability of finding it at each point around the nucleus. The arrangement of these electrons, described in Chapter 3, determines how an atom bonds to other atoms. Chemical reactions rearrange electrons; they never change the nucleus.


Neutral atoms
An atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its positive and negative charges cancel and it is electrically neutral. Atoms can, however, gain or lose electrons, and the particles that result are the subject of Section 2.4.

section: 2.3 Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
text:
2.3 Atomic number, mass number and isotopes

Atomic number defines the element
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom is its atomic number, symbol Z. The atomic number alone determines the element: every atom with one proton is hydrogen, every atom with six is carbon, every atom with eight is oxygen. The definition of an element given in Section 2.1 can therefore be made precise: an element is a substance whose atoms all have the same atomic number. At present 118 elements have been identified and named (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, n.d.).


Mass number
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus is its mass number, symbol A:
\[
A = Z + N
\]
where N is the number of neutrons. Because protons and neutrons have nearly the same mass and electrons are so light, the mass number is close to the mass of the atom measured in the unit introduced in Section 2.6.


Isotopes
Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but they can have different numbers of neutrons. Atoms that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called isotopes of the element. Isotopes of an element have almost identical chemical behaviour, because chemistry depends on the electrons, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom equals the number of protons.
An isotope is written with its mass number as a superscript before the symbol of the element, and sometimes with its atomic number as a subscript below it (Figure 2.3). In words, it is written as the name of the element followed by the mass number: carbon-12, carbon-13.






Figure 2.3: Isotope notation. The mass number A is written at the upper left of the element symbol and the atomic number Z at the lower left; the number of neutrons is A − Z. The three isotopes of carbon found in nature are shown below.



Hydrogen and carbon provide the two examples that matter most in this book.

Ordinary hydrogen, 1H, has a nucleus consisting of a single proton. Deuterium, 2H, has one proton and one neutron; in the international reference standard for ocean water it accounts for 0.0156 % of hydrogen atoms (IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights, n.d.-b). Tritium, 3H, has one proton and two neutrons; it is radioactive, with a half-life of 12.3 years (IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights, n.d.-b), and occurs only in traces.
Carbon-12 (six protons, six neutrons) makes up about 99 % of natural carbon (98.84 to 99.04 %, depending on the source), and carbon-13 (six protons, seven neutrons) about 1 % (IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights, n.d.-a). Carbon-14 (six protons, eight neutrons) is radioactive and occurs only in traces.



Stable and radioactive nuclei
Not every combination of protons and neutrons is stable. Protons repel one another electrically; they are held together, with the neutrons, by the strong nuclear force, which is much stronger than the electrical repulsion but acts only over distances about the size of a nucleus. A nucleus with too many or too few neutrons for its number of protons is unstable, and sooner or later transforms into a different nucleus, emitting radiation. This is the radioactive decay described in Chapter 1, and the half-lives of such nuclei range from fractions of a second to billions of years. Because decay proceeds at a fixed rate whatever the chemical surroundings, radioactive isotopes serve as clocks: the ages of rocks, and of the Earth itself, are measured from the amounts of radioactive isotopes and their decay products that they contain.

title: 2  What Matter Is Made Of
text:
2.4 Ions

Gaining and losing electrons
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons carries a net electric charge and is called an ion. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive; such an ion is called a cation. Gaining electrons gives a negative ion, called an anion. The charge is written as a superscript after the formula, as a multiple of e: a sodium atom that has lost one electron is the cation Na+, a magnesium atom that has lost two is Mg2+, and a chlorine atom that has gained one is the anion Cl−.
Only electrons are gained or lost when ions form. The nucleus is unchanged, so an ion of sodium is still sodium, with atomic number 11.


Ionic compounds
Positive and negative ions attract each other strongly. In solid sodium chloride, each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl− ions and each Cl− by six Na+, in a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a crystal lattice. A compound held together in this way is an ionic compound. It contains no separate molecules, and its formula, NaCl, gives only the ratio of the ions, which must balance so that the compound as a whole is neutral. Magnesium chloride, for example, has the formula MgCl2, because each Mg2+ ion needs two Cl− ions to balance its charge.


Ions made of several atoms
Some ions consist of several atoms bonded together and carrying a net charge as a whole. Such ions are called polyatomic ions. Three are important in the chemistry of life:

the hydroxide ion, OH−;
the ammonium ion, NH4+;
the phosphate ion, PO43−, a phosphorus atom surrounded by four oxygen atoms and carrying three negative charges.

Phosphate is a central component of RNA and DNA. Its negative charges, carried by every unit of these molecules, make them strongly charged in water, a property that governs how they dissolve, fold and interact with positive ions such as Mg2+.

title: 2  What Matter Is Made Of
text:
2.5 The periodic table

Arranging the elements
The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, in rows of different lengths, so that elements with similar chemical behaviour fall in the same column (Figure 2.4). A row is called a period, and a column a group. The groups are numbered from 1 to 18 from left to right. The regularity that the table displays was discovered in the nineteenth century from the chemical behaviour of the elements, before anything was known about the structure of atoms; its explanation in terms of electrons is given in Chapter 3.






Figure 2.4: The first four periods of the periodic table (elements 1 to 36). Each box shows the symbol and atomic number. Elements of the chemistry of life discussed in this book are highlighted: the five elements of RNA (orange), and sulfur, sodium, magnesium, potassium and chlorine (yellow).





Metals and non-metals
Most of the elements are metals: they conduct electricity and heat, have a characteristic lustre, and in compounds tend to lose electrons and form cations. Sodium, magnesium and iron are metals. The non-metals, grouped at the upper right of the table together with hydrogen, include hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine. Non-metals tend to gain electrons or, more often, to share them with other atoms, as described in Chapter 3. The elements in group 18, helium, neon, argon and their heavier relatives, are the noble gases; they hardly react at all.


The elements of life
Living matter is built mainly from a few light non-metals. Every molecule of RNA is made of only five elements: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and phosphorus. Proteins contain the same elements apart from phosphorus, together with sulfur. For the bacterium Escherichia coli, a standard laboratory organism, the dry mass (the mass remaining after all water has been removed) is about 47 % carbon (Heldal et al. 1985), 20 % oxygen, 14 % nitrogen, 8 % hydrogen and 3 % phosphorus (Neidhardt et al., n.d.). A small number of metal ions, such as sodium, potassium and magnesium, are present in smaller amounts but are essential.


Where the elements came from
Elements can be made only by nuclear reactions, which change the number of protons in a nucleus; ordinary chemistry cannot do this. Hydrogen and most of the helium in the Universe were formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and the heavier elements were formed later, inside stars, and were returned to space when those stars shed their outer layers or exploded. The carbon in every living cell was therefore made in stars that lived and died before the Sun and the Earth formed.

2.6 Weighing atoms

The atomic mass unit
The masses of atoms are far too small to be expressed conveniently in kilograms. Instead they are measured in the dalton (Da), also called the unified atomic mass unit (u). It is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a single atom of carbon-12, and equals 1.660 539 068 92 × 10−27 kg (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). On this scale an atom of carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 Da, and the mass of any atom in daltons is close to its mass number. A proton has a mass of 1.007 28 Da and a neutron 1.008 66 Da (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.).


Standard atomic weights
Most elements occur in nature as a mixture of isotopes. The average mass of the atoms of an element in a natural sample, expressed relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, is its atomic weight, also called its relative atomic mass. Because it is a ratio of two masses, it has no unit. The atomic weight of carbon is 12.011, slightly more than 12, because natural carbon contains about 1 % of carbon-13. The atomic weights of the elements are evaluated by the Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights of IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry; Table 2.2 lists the values for the elements used most in this book.

title: 2  What Matter Is Made Of
text:
Key points

A pure substance has a fixed composition; a mixture does not. Elements cannot be broken down chemically; compounds are made of elements in fixed proportions.
An atom is the smallest unit of an element; a molecule is a group of bonded atoms, the smallest unit of a molecular compound. A chemical formula such as H2O gives the number of atoms of each element.
Solid, liquid and gas differ in how closely and how freely the particles move, not in the particles themselves.
An atom has a nucleus of protons (+e) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (−e). The electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton; almost all the mass of an atom is in its tiny nucleus.
The atomic number Z (number of protons) defines the element. The mass number A is the number of protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A, and almost the same chemistry.
Ions are atoms or groups of atoms that have lost electrons (cations) or gained them (anions). Phosphate, PO43−, is a polyatomic anion found in RNA and DNA.
The periodic table orders the elements by atomic number, in periods (rows) and groups (columns) of similar behaviour. The elements of life are mainly light non-metals: H, C, N, O, P and S.
Atomic masses are measured in daltons (1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom). The atomic weight is the average for the natural isotope mixture; molecular masses are sums of atomic weights.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
The question of this chapter
Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom combine into a molecule of water, but helium atoms combine with nothing at all. Carbon forms four bonds, nitrogen three and oxygen two. This chapter asks: why do atoms join together, and what decides how many bonds each one forms? The answer lies in the arrangement of the electrons around the nucleus, and in particular in the electrons of the outermost shell.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.1 Electrons in shells

Energy levels
The electrons of an atom cannot have any energy whatever. They occupy a set of separate, fixed energy levels, determined by their attraction to the positive nucleus and their repulsion from one another. This is a result of quantum mechanics, and it can be confirmed directly: atoms absorb and emit light only at particular wavelengths, which correspond to the energy differences between their levels.
Energies on the scale of single atoms are conveniently measured in electronvolts (eV). One electronvolt is the energy gained by a particle carrying one elementary charge when it moves through an electric potential difference of one volt; it equals exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 J (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.-a).


Shells, subshells and orbitals
The region around the nucleus in which an electron of a given energy is likely to be found is called an orbital. An orbital is not a path. An electron in an atom does not travel along a fixed track; the orbital describes only where it is likely to be.
Orbitals are grouped into shells, numbered n = 1, 2, 3, and so on outwards from the nucleus. Electrons in higher shells are, on average, farther from the nucleus and less tightly held. Each shell is divided into subshells, labelled s, p, d and f: the first shell contains only an s subshell, the second contains s and p, and the third contains s, p and d. An s subshell has one orbital, which is spherical; a p subshell has three, each with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, pointing along three perpendicular directions (Figure 3.1).






Figure 3.1: Schematic shapes of an s orbital and the three p orbitals of a subshell, drawn as outlines of the region in which an electron is most likely to be found. The s orbital is spherical; the p orbitals point along three perpendicular axes, x, y and z.





How many electrons fit
Each orbital can hold at most two electrons. This rule, the Pauli exclusion principle, follows from a property of electrons called spin, which can take one of two values, often written “up” and “down”; two electrons can share an orbital only if their spins are opposite. It follows that an s subshell holds up to 2 electrons and a p subshell up to 6. The first shell, with only an s subshell, is full with 2 electrons. The second shell, with one s and three p orbitals, is full with 8.


Electron configurations
The electron configuration of an atom lists how many electrons occupy each subshell, written as the subshell label with the number of electrons as a superscript. In the most stable state of an atom, its ground state, electrons fill the lowest available levels first: 1s, then 2s, 2p, 3s and 3p. Valence electrons
The electrons in the outermost occupied shell are called valence electrons. They are the electrons farthest from the nucleus and the least tightly held, and they are the ones that take part in chemical bonding. The inner electrons, held close to the nucleus, are hardly affected by chemical reactions.
The periodic table (Chapter 2) is organised by valence electrons. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar chemistry. Nitrogen and phosphorus both have five; oxygen and sulfur both have six. This is the explanation, in terms of atomic structure, of the regularity that nineteenth-century chemists observed.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.2 Why atoms bond

Measuring how tightly electrons are held
The energy needed to remove one electron from a neutral atom in its ground state is called the first ionisation energy. It measures how tightly the atom holds its outermost electron, and it can be measured precisely from the light that atoms absorb. Figure 3.2 shows the values for the first eighteen elements.






Figure 3.2: First ionisation energies of the elements from hydrogen (Z = 1) to argon (Z = 18), from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database (Kramida et al. 2024). The elements of RNA are coloured. The peaks at helium, neon and argon correspond to full shells or subshells; the sharp drops at lithium and sodium mark the start of a new shell.



Two features stand out. The noble gases helium (24.59 eV), neon (21.56 eV) and argon (15.76 eV) hold their electrons more tightly than any other element in their rows. The elements that follow them, lithium (5.39 eV) and sodium (5.14 eV), hold their single outer electron most weakly (Kramida et al. 2024). An atom with a completely filled outer shell or subshell is unusually stable; an atom with one electron beyond a filled shell loses that electron easily.


The octet rule
This stability of filled shells explains much of chemistry. Atoms tend to react in ways that give each of them the electron arrangement of the nearest noble gas: two electrons in the first shell for hydrogen, and eight in the outermost shell for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and their heavier relatives. The tendency to reach eight valence electrons is called the octet rule. It is a rule of thumb rather than a law, and it has exceptions, phosphorus among them, but it predicts correctly the bonding of most of the molecules in this book.
An atom can reach a noble-gas arrangement in two ways: by transferring electrons to or from another atom, or by sharing electrons with it. The first gives ionic bonds, the second covalent bonds.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.3 Ionic bonds
A sodium atom has one valence electron, beyond the filled shells of neon. A chlorine atom has seven valence electrons, one short of the eight of argon. When sodium and chlorine react, each sodium atom transfers its outer electron to a chlorine atom:
\[
\text{Na} + \text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}
\]
Both ions now have noble-gas arrangements: Na+ that of neon and Cl− that of argon. The oppositely charged ions attract each other and pack together into a crystal. The attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. Ionic bonding is typical of compounds between a metal, which loses electrons easily, and a non-metal, which gains them readily.
Ionic bonds are not directional: each ion attracts every neighbour of opposite charge, whatever its direction. Ionic compounds therefore form extended crystals rather than separate molecules, and many dissolve in water, where the ions separate, as Chapter 5 explains.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.4 Covalent bonds

Sharing a pair of electrons
Two non-metal atoms both tend to gain electrons, so neither gives one up to the other. Instead, they share. A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. The shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei at once, and this attraction holds the atoms together.
The simplest example is the hydrogen molecule, H2. Each hydrogen atom brings one electron. In the molecule, the two electrons occupy the region between the nuclei and are counted by both atoms, so each atom has two electrons around it, the arrangement of helium. The distance between the two nuclei, the bond length, is 0.741 Å (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022), where the ångström (Å) equals 10−10 m. The covalent bonds between the atoms of the molecules in this book are all between about 1 and 2 Å long.


How many bonds each atom forms
An atom forms as many covalent bonds as it needs electrons to complete its octet, or its pair in the case of hydrogen. This gives the characteristic number of bonds, or valence, of each element:

hydrogen, with 1 valence electron, needs 1 more and forms 1 bond;
oxygen, with 6, needs 2 more and forms 2 bonds;
nitrogen, with 5, needs 3 more and forms 3 bonds;
carbon, with 4, needs 4 more and forms 4 bonds.

These four numbers, 1, 2, 3 and 4 for H, O, N and C, are worth memorising: they decide the structure of every organic molecule. Methane, CH4, has one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms; ammonia, NH3, one nitrogen bonded to three; and water, H2O, one oxygen bonded to two.


Lewis structures
A Lewis structure is a drawing that shows how the valence electrons of a molecule are arranged. Each shared pair of electrons is drawn as a line between two atoms, and each unshared pair as two dots on the atom that carries it (Figure 3.3). An unshared pair of valence electrons, which belongs to one atom only, is called a lone pair. In water, the oxygen atom forms two bonds and carries two lone pairs; in ammonia, the nitrogen forms three bonds and carries one lone pair. Counting the electrons around oxygen in water, two shared pairs and two lone pairs, gives eight, an octet.






Figure 3.3: Lewis structures of hydrogen, methane, ammonia, water, nitrogen and hydrogen cyanide. Each line is a shared pair of electrons (a covalent bond); each pair of dots is a lone pair. Three parallel lines mark a triple bond. Every atom except hydrogen is surrounded by eight electrons; hydrogen by two.



Lone pairs are not inert decoration. They give water and ammonia much of their chemical behaviour: a lone pair can accept a hydrogen ion, H+, as in the formation of the ammonium ion NH4+, and it can take part in the weak attractions called hydrogen bonds, described in Chapter 5.


Phosphorus: an exception that matters
Phosphorus has five valence electrons, like nitrogen, and in some compounds it forms three bonds, as the octet rule predicts. In phosphate and its compounds, however, the phosphorus atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and the usual Lewis structure draws five bonds to it: one double bond to oxygen and three single bonds. Atoms of the third period, such as phosphorus and sulfur, are commonly drawn with more than eight electrons around them in such structures. Whatever the details of the description, the facts are clear: the phosphorus atom of a phosphate group is bonded to four oxygen atoms arranged at the corners of a tetrahedron, and the group as a whole carries negative charge in water.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.5 Double and triple bonds

More than one shared pair
Two atoms can share more than one pair of electrons. Two shared pairs form a double bond, drawn as two lines, and three shared pairs a triple bond, drawn as three lines. The number of shared pairs between two atoms is called the bond order.
Multiple bonds allow atoms to complete their octets with fewer partners. In carbon dioxide, O=C=O, the carbon atom forms two double bonds, which count as four bonds, and each oxygen forms one double bond, which counts as two. In the nitrogen molecule, N\(\equiv\)N, the two atoms share three pairs, and each also carries one lone pair. In formaldehyde, H2C=O, carbon forms two single bonds to hydrogen and one double bond to oxygen. In hydrogen cyanide, H–C\(\equiv\)N, carbon forms a single bond to hydrogen and a triple bond to nitrogen. Formaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide are two of the simplest compounds of carbon, and both are considered important starting materials in many proposed routes to the building blocks of life.


Shorter and stronger
Each additional shared pair pulls the two atoms closer together. The three simplest compounds of carbon and hydrogen with two carbon atoms show this directly. In ethane, C2H6, the carbon atoms are joined by a single bond of length 1.536 Å; in ethylene, C2H4, by a double bond of 1.339 Å; and in acetylene, C2H2, by a triple bond of 1.203 Å (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022).
Multiple bonds are also stronger. The strength of a bond is measured by the bond enthalpy, the energy needed to break the bond in the gas phase, given for one mole of such bonds (the mole is defined in Chapter 6). Table 3.2 gives some values. The triple bond of N2 is more than twice as strong as any of the single bonds in the table, which is why the nitrogen gas of the atmosphere is so unreactive.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
3.6 The shapes of molecules

Electron pairs keep apart
Molecules have definite three-dimensional shapes, and shape matters: it decides which molecules can fit against which, and therefore how they react and how they recognise one another. The shape of a small molecule can be predicted from one principle. The electron pairs around a central atom, both bonding pairs and lone pairs, repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. This is the valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model.

Four electron pairs point towards the corners of a tetrahedron, a solid with four triangular faces. The angle between any two of them is 109.47°.
Three groups of electrons lie in a plane, at 120° to each other (trigonal planar). A double bond counts as one group.
Two groups lie on opposite sides of the central atom, at 180° (linear).



Methane, ammonia and water
Methane, ammonia and water each have four electron pairs around the central atom, so all three are based on the tetrahedron (Figure 3.4). In methane all four pairs are bonds, and the molecule is a regular tetrahedron with H–C–H angles of 109.47°. In ammonia one pair is a lone pair; the three hydrogen atoms form a low pyramid, with H–N–H angles of 106.67°. In water two pairs are lone pairs, and the molecule is bent, with an H–O–H angle of 104.48° (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022). Lone pairs spread out more than bonding pairs and push the bonds slightly closer together, which is why the angle shrinks from methane to water.






Figure 3.4: Shapes of methane, ammonia and water, with measured bond angles (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022). In all three, four electron pairs around the central atom point approximately to the corners of a tetrahedron; lone pairs are shown as shaded lobes. A wedge-shaped bond points towards the viewer and a dashed bond away from the viewer.





Flat and straight molecules
When the central atom has a double bond, the number of groups around it falls to three, and the molecule becomes flat. Formaldehyde, H2C=O, and ethylene, H2C=CH2, are planar, with angles close to 120°; in ethylene the measured angles are 117.6° for H–C–H and 121.2° for H–C–C (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022). With two groups, as in carbon dioxide (O=C=O) and hydrogen cyanide (H–C\(\equiv\)N), the molecule is linear.


Hybrid orbitals, briefly
The tetrahedral shape of methane raises a puzzle: carbon’s valence electrons occupy one spherical 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals at right angles, none of which points to the corners of a tetrahedron. Chemists resolve this with the idea of hybrid orbitals, mathematical combinations of s and p orbitals that point in the directions of the bonds. A carbon atom forming four single bonds is described by four sp3 hybrids (tetrahedral); one forming a double bond by three sp2 hybrids (planar, 120°); and one forming a triple bond by two sp hybrids (linear, 180°). The labels sp3, sp2 and sp are used widely in chemistry as a shorthand for these three geometries of carbon.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
section: 3.7 Carbon, the element of chains and rings
text:
3.7 Carbon, the element of chains and rings
The bonding rules of this chapter explain why carbon, rather than any other element, forms the backbone of the molecules of life. A carbon atom forms four bonds, more than any other light element, and it bonds strongly to other carbon atoms as well as to hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Carbon atoms can therefore link into chains and rings of almost any length and shape, with other atoms attached at every position. The four bonds of each carbon point in different directions, so these chains and rings are three-dimensional.
Compounds built on frameworks of carbon atoms are called organic compounds, and their chemistry is organic chemistry. The name dates from a time when such compounds were thought to be made only by living organisms; since the nineteenth century they have been made in the laboratory from inorganic materials, beginning with Friedrich Wöhler’s synthesis of urea in 1828 (Wöhler 1828), and the name now refers only to their composition. The sugars, the nucleobases and RNA itself are all organic compounds. Chapter 4 shows how their structures are drawn, and Chapter 11 how their parts behave.

title: 3  Electrons and Bonds
text:
Key points

Electrons occupy fixed energy levels, grouped into shells (n = 1, 2, 3, …) and subshells (s, p, d). Each orbital holds at most two electrons; the first shell is full with 2 electrons and the second with 8.
Valence electrons, in the outermost shell, take part in bonding: H 1, C 4, N 5, O 6, P 5. Elements in the same group have the same number.
Filled shells are especially stable, as shown by the high ionisation energies of the noble gases. Atoms tend to reach a noble-gas arrangement (the octet rule).
In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred, and oppositely charged ions attract each other. In a covalent bond, a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
Hydrogen forms 1 covalent bond, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3 and carbon 4. Lewis structures show bonds as lines and lone pairs as dots.
Double and triple bonds share two and three pairs; they are shorter and stronger than single bonds (C–C 1.536 Å, C=C 1.339 Å, C\(\equiv\)C 1.203 Å). The N\(\equiv\)N bond, 945.4 kJ mol−1, makes nitrogen gas unreactive.
Electron pairs around an atom keep as far apart as possible (VSEPR). Four pairs give tetrahedral directions: methane is tetrahedral (109.47°), ammonia pyramidal (106.67°) and water bent (104.48°). Three groups give planar molecules, two give linear ones.
Carbon’s four bonds and its strong bonds to itself allow chains and rings: the basis of organic chemistry.
