title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
The question of this chapter
Open any book or paper on the chemistry of life and you will find pages covered with hexagons, zigzag lines and letters. These drawings are the language in which chemists describe molecules, and they carry more information than any amount of text. This chapter asks: how is a molecule drawn, and how can a drawing be read? It introduces the main types of chemical formula, explains the conventions of the skeletal formula used in almost all modern chemistry, and shows how three-dimensional shape is represented on a flat page. By the end of the chapter, you should be able to look at the drawing of a sugar or a nucleobase and count every atom in it.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
4.1 One molecule, many drawings

Why the molecular formula is not enough
Chapter 2 introduced the chemical formula, such as H2O for water. A formula that gives only the number of atoms of each element in a molecule is called a molecular formula. For small molecules it is often all that is needed: there is only one way to join two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom so that each forms its usual number of bonds.
For larger molecules, the molecular formula is not enough. The formula C2H6O describes two different compounds. In ethanol, the alcohol of wine and beer, the two carbon atoms are bonded to each other and the oxygen is bonded to one of them and to a hydrogen atom. In dimethyl ether, the oxygen sits between the two carbon atoms. Both arrangements obey the bonding rules of Chapter 3 (carbon 4 bonds, oxygen 2, hydrogen 1), but they are different substances with different properties: at atmospheric pressure ethanol boils at 78 °C and is a liquid at room temperature, whereas dimethyl ether boils at −24 °C and is a gas (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers (Figure 4.1). They are the reason why chemistry needs drawings.






Figure 4.1: Ethanol and dimethyl ether, two isomers with the molecular formula C2H6O, drawn as full structural formulas. All atoms and all bonds are shown. The only difference is the position of the oxygen atom, but it gives two different compounds.





Four ways to draw ethanol
Chemists use several types of formula, which show the same molecule with different amounts of detail. Figure 4.2 shows ethanol in four of them.

The molecular formula, C2H6O, gives the composition only.
A structural formula shows every atom and every bond as in a Lewis structure, usually omitting the lone pairs.
A condensed formula, CH3CH2OH, writes the atoms in the order in which they are connected, grouping each carbon with the hydrogen atoms attached to it.
A skeletal formula shows the carbon framework as a zigzag of lines and leaves out the carbon atoms and the hydrogen atoms bonded to them.







Figure 4.2: Ethanol in four representations: molecular formula, full structural formula, condensed formula and skeletal formula. All four describe the same molecule; each successive form leaves more to be understood by the reader.



Each type has its uses. The molecular formula is used to calculate masses (Chapter 6). The structural formula is the clearest for small molecules and for showing exactly which bonds change in a reaction. The condensed formula fits into a line of text. The skeletal formula is the most compact for large molecules, and it is the form in which almost all molecules in modern chemistry and biochemistry are drawn.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
4.2 Structural and condensed formulas

Structural formulas
A full structural formula is a Lewis structure in which the lone pairs are usually left out. Every bond appears as a line: one line for a single bond, two for a double bond, three for a triple bond. To check a structural formula, count the lines at each atom. Every carbon must have four, every nitrogen three, every oxygen two and every hydrogen one, unless the atom carries a charge (Section 4.4).
The angles in a structural formula are not the real bond angles. A carbon atom with four single bonds is drawn as a cross with 90° angles for convenience, although in the molecule its bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart (Chapter 3). A structural formula shows which atoms are connected, not the shape of the molecule.


Condensed formulas
A condensed formula lists the atoms along the main chain from one end to the other, writing each carbon followed by the hydrogen atoms attached to it. CH3CH2OH is read as: a carbon carrying three hydrogens, bonded to a carbon carrying two hydrogens, bonded to an oxygen carrying one hydrogen. Dimethyl ether is CH3OCH3. Bonds within the chain are not drawn, although double and triple bonds are often shown: ethylene is CH2=CH2 and hydrogen cyanide HC\(\equiv\)N.
Groups attached to the chain as branches are written in parentheses after the atom that carries them. Acetone, a common solvent, is CH3C(O)CH3 or (CH3)2CO: a central carbon bonded to two CH3 groups and double-bonded to an oxygen. A subscript after parentheses means that the group appears that many times.
The condensed formula of a group that recurs in many molecules soon becomes familiar. CH3– is a methyl group, –OH a hydroxy group, and –COOH a carboxy group (a carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an –OH). Chapter 11 describes these and other functional groups and the chemistry they bring.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
4.3 Skeletal formulas

The four rules
Large molecules contain dozens of carbon and hydrogen atoms, and drawing each one would bury the structure in letters. The skeletal formula avoids this. It is drawn according to four rules.

Bonds are lines. Single bonds are drawn as single lines, double bonds as two parallel lines, triple bonds as three.
Every corner and every line end is a carbon atom, unless another atom is written there. Chains of carbon atoms are drawn as zigzags, so that each carbon atom appears as a corner.
Hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not drawn. Each carbon is understood to carry as many hydrogen atoms as it needs to make four bonds in total.
All other atoms are written with their symbols, together with any hydrogen atoms attached to them: O, OH, N, NH2, P and so on.

The zigzag of rule 2 has a physical basis: in a chain of carbon atoms with tetrahedral bonds, the stretched-out shape of the chain really is a zigzag, with angles close to 109.5°. Skeletal formulas are drawn with 120° angles, which makes the zigzag regular on paper.


Reading a skeletal formula
To read a skeletal formula, find every carbon atom and work out its hydrogen atoms. For each corner or line end without a symbol, count the lines that meet there; the number of hydrogen atoms is four minus the number of bonds, counting a double bond as two and a triple bond as three. Figure 4.3 shows the procedure for several molecules, with the hidden hydrogen atoms written in grey.






Figure 4.3: Reading skeletal formulas. Top row: skeletal formulas of butane, propan-1-ol, but-2-ene and acetic acid. Bottom row: the same molecules with every carbon atom labelled and the hydrogen atoms that the skeletal formula leaves out written in grey. A line end is a CH3 group, a corner with two lines is a CH2 group, and a carbon with a double bond and one other bond is a CH group.



Three patterns appear so often that they are worth recognising at a glance:

a line end is a CH3 group (one bond, so three hydrogen atoms);
a corner where two single lines meet is a CH2 group;
a corner where three single lines meet is a CH group, and one where four meet is a carbon with no hydrogen.

A carbon atom that forms a double bond and one single bond, as in but-2-ene, carries one hydrogen; a carbon atom double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to two other atoms, as in acetone or acetic acid, carries none.


Rings
Carbon chains can close into rings, and skeletal formulas show rings as polygons. A hexagon with no symbols at its corners is cyclohexane, C6H12: six carbon atoms, each a corner with two lines, and so each carrying two hydrogen atoms. Rings can contain atoms other than carbon, such as oxygen or nitrogen; these are written at the corner they occupy. A ring containing at least one atom other than carbon is called a heterocycle. The sugar of RNA and the four nucleobases are all heterocycles.


A worked example: ribose
The sugar in RNA is ribose, C5H10O5. In RNA it is present as a five-membered ring of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom. Figure 4.4 shows its skeletal formula and the same drawing with every hidden atom made explicit.






Figure 4.4: The sugar ribose (in its five-membered ring form), as a skeletal formula (left) and with every carbon and hydrogen atom shown (right). The carbon atoms are numbered 1 to 5 according to the standard convention for sugars. Counting gives 5 carbon atoms, 10 hydrogen atoms and 5 oxygen atoms: C5H10O5.



The count proceeds corner by corner. The ring has five corners: one is labelled O, so the other four are carbon atoms. A fifth carbon atom is the line end outside the ring, bonded to an OH group. Each of the five carbon atoms then receives hydrogen atoms to make up four bonds. The carbon atom numbered 1 is bonded to the ring oxygen, to carbon 2 and to an OH group, so it carries one hydrogen. Carbons 2, 3 and 4 are each bonded to two ring neighbours and to one other group, and also carry one hydrogen each. Carbon 5 is bonded to carbon 4 and to an OH group, and carries two hydrogens. Adding the hydrogen atoms of the four OH groups gives 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 10 hydrogen atoms, and the oxygen atoms number 4 in OH groups plus 1 in the ring, giving 5. The molecular formula is C5H10O5.
The numbering of the carbon atoms is part of the language of biochemistry. In a sugar, carbon 1 is the carbon that carries two bonds to oxygen atoms (here the ring oxygen and an OH group), and the numbering continues along the chain. When the sugar is part of a larger molecule such as RNA, its carbon numbers receive a prime, written 1\('\), 2\('\), 3\('\) and so on, to distinguish them from the numbered atoms of the attached nucleobase. Chapter 12 uses this numbering to describe how the parts of RNA are joined.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
section: 4.4 Charges and lone pairs in drawings
text:
4.4 Charges and lone pairs in drawings
Atoms in a drawing occasionally carry a charge. An oxygen atom that forms only one bond and carries three lone pairs has one electron more than a neutral oxygen atom in a molecule, and is written O−. A nitrogen atom that forms four bonds, as in the ammonium ion, has given part of its lone pair to the fourth bond and is written N+. Such a charge, assigned to an individual atom in a structure, is called a formal charge. The rule for bond counts given in Section 4.2 is therefore modified: an O− forms one bond and an N+ forms four.
The phosphate groups of RNA are usually drawn with one or two O− atoms, because at the acidity of most natural waters they have lost hydrogen ions, as Chapter 8 explains. When a phosphate is drawn as P bonded to four O atoms, one of them by a double line and one or more of them carrying a minus sign, this is the convention being used.
Lone pairs are usually omitted from skeletal formulas, but every oxygen and nitrogen atom still has them. A neutral oxygen with two bonds has two lone pairs, and a neutral nitrogen with three bonds has one. These lone pairs take part in many reactions and in the hydrogen bonds of Chapter 5, so a reader should learn to imagine them even when they are not drawn.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
4.5 Three dimensions on paper

Wedges and dashes
Molecules are three-dimensional, and some of their properties depend on the arrangement of atoms in space, not only on which atoms are connected. To show this arrangement, chemists use two kinds of special bond. A solid wedge, widening towards one atom, represents a bond pointing out of the page towards the viewer. A dashed (hashed) bond represents a bond pointing behind the page, away from the viewer. Ordinary lines lie in the plane of the page. With these three kinds of line, the tetrahedral arrangement around a carbon atom can be drawn as two ordinary bonds in the plane, one wedge and one dash, as in the shapes of methane, ammonia and water in Chapter 3.
The arrangement in space matters most when a carbon atom carries four different groups. Such a carbon can exist in two arrangements that are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed, like a left and a right hand. Chapter 11 explains this property, called chirality, and why the sugar of RNA occurs in only one of its mirror-image forms.


Drawing sugar rings: the Haworth projection
Rings of sugars are often drawn in a special perspective called a Haworth projection (Figure 4.5). The ring is drawn flat, in a plane roughly perpendicular to the page, as if seen obliquely from above; the lower edge is often drawn thicker to indicate that it is nearer to the viewer. The ring oxygen is placed at the back, behind the plane of the page (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, n.d.). Each carbon atom in the ring has two remaining bonds, which are drawn as vertical lines, one pointing up and one pointing down. The groups on these lines, OH or H, are placed above or below the plane of the ring.






Figure 4.5: Two representations of ribose in its five-membered ring form. Left: a skeletal formula with wedges (towards the viewer) and dashes (away from the viewer). Right: a Haworth projection, in which the ring is seen obliquely and the thick lower edge is nearest to the viewer; groups are placed above or below the plane of the ring. In both, the OH groups on carbons 2 and 3 lie on the same side of the ring, below it in the Haworth projection, and the CH2OH group (carbon 5) lies above it.



The Haworth projection makes it easy to see which groups lie on the same side of the ring. In ribose, the hydroxy groups on carbons 2 and 3 point to the same side, and this arrangement is one of the features that distinguish ribose from other sugars with the same formula, C5H10O5. The ring is not really flat; five-membered rings are slightly puckered. The Haworth projection is a convention for showing the relative positions of groups, not the exact shape.


Ball-and-stick and space-filling models
Computer graphics and physical models show molecules in other ways. In a ball-and-stick model, atoms are spheres and bonds are rods; the model shows bond angles correctly and makes the three-dimensional arrangement clear. In a space-filling model, each atom is drawn as a sphere of roughly its real size, and the spheres overlap; the model shows the overall shape and surface of the molecule, which decides how it fits against other molecules. Models of large biological molecules often use further simplifications, such as ribbons that trace the backbone of an RNA or protein chain.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
section: 4.6 Flat rings with alternating double bonds
text:
4.6 Flat rings with alternating double bonds

Benzene
A ring of six carbon atoms with alternating single and double bonds is benzene, C6H6. The ring structure was proposed by August Kekulé in 1865 (Kekulé 1865), and it raised a puzzle: if the bonds alternated, the double bonds should be shorter than the single bonds, yet all six carbon-carbon bonds in benzene are found to have the same length, 1.397 Å (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022), between the lengths of a single and a double bond (Chapter 3).
The explanation is that benzene cannot be described by a single Lewis structure. Two structures can be drawn, differing only in the positions of the double bonds, and the real molecule is a blend of the two, with the six electrons of the three double bonds spread evenly around the whole ring (Figure 4.6). This situation, in which a molecule is described by two or more Lewis structures that differ only in the placement of electrons, is called resonance. Benzene is sometimes drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside, to show the evenly spread electrons, but the form with alternating double bonds is more common, and it must be understood as one of two equivalent drawings.






Figure 4.6: Benzene. Left: the two equivalent structures with alternating double bonds; the double-headed arrow indicates resonance, not a reaction. Right: the representation with a circle, showing the six electrons spread evenly around the ring. All six carbon-carbon bonds have the same length, 1.397 Å.





Aromatic rings
Benzene and other flat rings with electrons spread evenly around them in this way are called aromatic. (The name is historical: many early-known compounds of this kind had strong smells.) Aromatic rings are flat and unusually stable. Many contain nitrogen atoms in the ring. The four nucleobases of RNA, adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil, all contain flat, aromatic heterocycles with nitrogen atoms (Figure 4.7). Their flatness allows them to stack on top of each other in a strand of RNA, and the nitrogen and oxygen atoms on their edges form the hydrogen bonds that pair bases with each other. Both properties are described in Chapters 5 and 12.






Figure 4.7: Adenine, one of the four nucleobases of RNA, as a skeletal formula (left) and with all atoms shown (right). It contains two fused aromatic rings, a six-membered and a five-membered ring, with nitrogen atoms at five ring positions. Counting gives C5H5N5.

title: 4  Reading Molecular Drawings
text:
Key points

A molecular formula gives composition only. Isomers, such as ethanol and dimethyl ether (both C2H6O), have the same molecular formula but different structures and properties.
A structural formula shows every atom and bond; a condensed formula such as CH3CH2OH lists atoms in order of connection; a skeletal formula shows the carbon framework only.
In a skeletal formula, every corner and line end is a carbon atom, hydrogen atoms on carbon are omitted, and each carbon carries enough hydrogen atoms to make four bonds. All other atoms are written with their hydrogen atoms.
A line end is CH3, a corner with two single lines is CH2, and one with three is CH.
Rings are drawn as polygons; rings containing atoms other than carbon are heterocycles. Ribose, C5H10O5, has a five-membered ring of four carbons and one oxygen; its carbons are numbered 1 to 5, and 1\('\) to 5\('\) when the sugar is part of a larger molecule.
An O− forms one bond and an N+ four; such formal charges appear on phosphate groups and ammonium groups.
Wedges point towards the viewer and dashes away. Haworth projections show sugar rings obliquely, with groups above or below the ring.
Benzene is a flat ring whose six electrons of the double bonds are spread around the ring (resonance). Such aromatic rings, often containing nitrogen, form the nucleobases of RNA.

title: 5  Polarity, Hydrogen Bonds and Water
text:
The question of this chapter
Water and methane are molecules of almost the same mass. At room temperature methane is a gas that boils at −162 °C, whereas water is a liquid that boils only at 100 °C. Salt and sugar dissolve in water but not in oil. Ice floats. This chapter asks: what makes water so different, and what holds molecules together when no chemical bond joins them? The answer starts with a single property of atoms, electronegativity, and leads to the hydrogen bond, the interaction that holds the two strands of DNA together and gives RNA its shapes.
crumbs: 5  Polarity, Hydrogen Bonds and Water

title: 5  Polarity, Hydrogen Bonds and Water
text:
5.1 Unequal sharing

Electronegativity
In the hydrogen molecule, H2, the two atoms are identical and share their electron pair equally. When two different atoms are bonded, this is generally not so: one atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the other, and the electrons spend more time near it. The tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons towards itself is called its electronegativity, often written with the Greek letter \(\chi\) (chi).
Electronegativity is not measured directly, like a mass. It is derived from measured bond energies by a procedure introduced by Linus Pauling in 1932 (Pauling 1932), and the values are pure numbers on what is called the Pauling scale. Table 5.1 gives the values for the elements of this book.



Table 5.1: Pauling electronegativities (Allred 1961).

Two trends are visible. Across a row of the periodic table, electronegativity increases from left to right, as the nuclear charge increases while the valence electrons stay in the same shell. Down a column it decreases, because the valence electrons lie farther from the nucleus: phosphorus (2.19) is much less electronegative than nitrogen (3.04), although both have five valence electrons. Of the elements of life, oxygen and nitrogen are by far the most electronegative. Carbon, hydrogen and phosphorus lie close together, between 2.19 and 2.55.


Polar bonds
A covalent bond in which the electrons are shared unequally is a polar bond. Its more electronegative end carries a small excess of negative charge, and the other end a small deficit. These partial charges are written \(\delta\)− and \(\delta\)+ (\(\delta\), the Greek letter delta, is read “a fraction of”), to distinguish them from the whole-number charges of ions. The larger the difference in electronegativity, the more polar the bond. A C–H bond (difference 0.35) is nearly non-polar. An O–H bond (difference 1.24) is strongly polar, with the negative end on oxygen, and so are N–H, C=O and P–O bonds.
When the difference becomes very large, as between sodium (0.93) and chlorine (3.16), the electron is not shared at all but effectively transferred, and the result is a pair of ions (Chapter 3). Covalent and ionic bonds are therefore two ends of a continuous range. Non-polar covalent bonds lie at one end, ionic bonds at the other, and polar covalent bonds in between.


Polar molecules
A molecule as a whole is polar if the partial charges of its bonds do not cancel, so that one side of the molecule is slightly negative and the other slightly positive. Whether this happens depends on the shape of the molecule as well as on its bonds. A molecule with separated positive and negative charge is said to have a dipole, and the size of the separation is measured by its dipole moment, given in a unit called the debye (D).
Water is bent (Chapter 3), so the two O–H bond dipoles point partly in the same direction and add up: water has a dipole moment of 1.857 D, with its negative end at the oxygen atom (Figure 5.1). Ammonia, also not symmetric, has 1.476 D. Carbon dioxide, O=C=O, has two strongly polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is straight, so they point in exactly opposite directions and cancel; carbon dioxide has no dipole moment. Methane is also non-polar, because its four slightly polar C–H bonds point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel exactly (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022).






Figure 5.1: Polarity of the water molecule. Each O–H bond is polar, with partial negative charge (\(\delta\)−) on oxygen and partial positive charge (\(\delta\)+) on hydrogen. Because the molecule is bent, the two bond dipoles add to a net dipole moment of 1.857 D (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2022).

title: 5  Polarity, Hydrogen Bonds and Water
text:
5.2 Forces between molecules

Bonds within molecules and forces between them
Covalent bonds hold the atoms of a molecule together. Molecules also attract one another, but by much weaker intermolecular forces. These forces do not create new molecules, and at ordinary temperatures they are constantly broken and re-formed as the molecules move. They nevertheless decide whether a substance is a gas, a liquid or a solid at a given temperature, and whether it dissolves in water. All intermolecular forces are electrical in origin: they arise from the attraction between regions of positive and negative charge on neighbouring molecules.


Dipole-dipole and dispersion forces
Polar molecules attract each other because the positive end of one is drawn towards the negative end of another. This is a dipole-dipole interaction.
Non-polar molecules attract each other too, more weakly. The electron cloud of any molecule fluctuates, so that at any instant it may have a small, temporary dipole. That dipole distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule, creating a dipole in it, and the two temporary dipoles attract. This is the dispersion force, also called the London force. It acts between all molecules, and it is larger for larger molecules, which have more electrons. Dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, with related interactions, are together called van der Waals forces.


The hydrogen bond
One intermolecular interaction is of special importance for water and for the molecules of life. IUPAC defines it as follows: “The hydrogen bond is an attractive interaction between a hydrogen atom from a molecule or a molecular fragment X–H in which X is more electronegative than H, and an atom or a group of atoms in the same or a different molecule, in which there is evidence of bond formation” (Arunan et al. 2011).
In practice, a hydrogen bond forms when a hydrogen atom bonded to oxygen or nitrogen, and so carrying a \(\delta\)+ charge, points towards a lone pair on another oxygen or nitrogen atom (Figure 5.2). It is written X–H···Y, with the dotted line for the hydrogen bond. The group X–H is the hydrogen-bond donor, and the atom Y with its lone pair is the hydrogen-bond acceptor. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than other intermolecular forces, but much weaker than covalent bonds, so they are made and broken easily at ordinary temperatures. They are also directional: they are strongest when X, H and Y lie on a straight line (Arunan et al. 2011).






Figure 5.2: A hydrogen bond between two water molecules. The O–H group of the left-hand molecule (the donor) points towards a lone pair on the oxygen atom of the right-hand molecule (the acceptor). Covalent bonds are drawn as solid lines and the hydrogen bond as a dotted line. Schematic; distances not to scale.



Hydrogen bonds are not limited to water. They form wherever O–H or N–H groups meet oxygen or nitrogen atoms with lone pairs: between molecules of alcohols, sugars and nucleobases, and between different parts of the same large molecule. The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases, and the same kind of pairing folds a single strand of RNA into a shape. Chapter 12 shows which atoms form these bonds.


Evidence from boiling points
When a liquid boils, its molecules separate from one another, so a higher boiling point indicates stronger intermolecular forces. Table 5.2 compares four small molecules containing hydrogen.

Hydrogen sulfide, H2S, is nearly twice as heavy as water, but sulfur (2.58) is much less electronegative than oxygen (3.44), and H2S forms only weak hydrogen bonds; it boils 160 °C lower than water. Hydrogen fluoride, which contains the most electronegative element of all, also boils unusually high for its size.

title: 5  Polarity, Hydrogen Bonds and Water
text:
5.3 Water, the solvent of life

A small molecule with four hydrogen-bonding sites
A water molecule is small, bent and polar. Its oxygen atom carries two lone pairs and is bonded to two hydrogen atoms, so each molecule can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept two. In liquid water, each molecule is linked to its neighbours by a network of hydrogen bonds that are constantly broken and re-formed. This network is responsible for the unusually high boiling point of water, and for most of its other unusual properties.


Solutions
A solution is a mixture in which one substance is spread evenly through another at the level of individual molecules or ions. The substance present in the larger amount, usually a liquid, is the solvent; the substance dissolved in it is the solute. A solution in which water is the solvent is an aqueous solution. The maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature is its solubility.
A useful rule of thumb is “like dissolves like”. Polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents, such as water, and non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents, such as oils. A molecule that can form hydrogen bonds with water, such as an alcohol, a sugar or a nucleobase, can take a place in the hydrogen-bond network of water and dissolves well. Table sugar dissolves in water in large amounts for this reason: each of its molecules carries eight O–H groups.


Dissolving ions
Water also dissolves many ionic compounds, such as sodium chloride, which do not dissolve in oils. Two properties of water are responsible.
First, water greatly weakens the electrical force between charges. The force between two charges in a medium is smaller than in a vacuum by a factor called the relative permittivity of the medium. For liquid water at 25 °C, the relative permittivity is 78.4 (International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam 2011): the attraction between a sodium ion and a chloride ion in water is almost eighty times weaker than at the same distance in a vacuum, and the ions can drift apart.
Second, water molecules arrange themselves around each dissolved ion, forming a hydration shell (Figure 5.3). Around a positive ion, such as Na+, the water molecules turn their \(\delta\)− oxygen atoms towards the ion; around a negative ion, such as Cl−, they turn their \(\delta\)+ hydrogen atoms towards it. The attraction between the ion and these oriented water molecules holds the ion in solution.






Figure 5.3: Hydration of ions (schematic). Water molecules around a sodium ion (left) point their partially negative oxygen atoms towards the positive ion; those around a chloride ion (right) point their partially positive hydrogen atoms towards the negative ion. Only one layer of water molecules is shown, in two dimensions.





The hydrophobic effect
Non-polar molecules, such as the hydrocarbons of oil, dissolve poorly in water and tend to cluster together when placed in it; oil and water separate. This is the hydrophobic effect (from the Greek for “water-fearing”). It is not caused by a special attraction between the non-polar molecules. A non-polar molecule cannot form hydrogen bonds, and the water molecules around it are restricted in the hydrogen bonds they can form with one another. When the non-polar molecules cluster together, less of their surface touches water, and fewer water molecules are restricted. Polar and charged groups, which interact favourably with water, are called hydrophilic (“water-loving”); non-polar groups are hydrophobic.
Some molecules have a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part. Such molecules are called amphiphilic. Soap is an example: a long hydrocarbon tail attached to a charged head. In water, amphiphilic molecules arrange themselves with their tails together, away from the water, and their heads facing outwards. Depending on their shape, they form small spherical clusters or double layers that close into hollow spheres. The membranes that surround every living cell are such double layers, and similar structures formed from simple amphiphilic molecules are studied as possible compartments for the first cells.


Some unusual properties of water
The hydrogen-bond network gives water several properties that are unusual for so small a molecule.

Ice floats. In ice, every water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a regular, open, tetrahedral arrangement, which occupies more space than the disordered liquid. At 0 °C and atmospheric pressure, ice has a density of 916.7 kg m−3 and liquid water 999.8 kg m−3 (Feistel and Wagner 2006; Wagner and Pruß 2002). Because ice is less dense, it floats, and bodies of water freeze from the top down, leaving liquid water beneath.
Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C. As it cools below this temperature, the liquid begins to form open, ice-like arrangements and expands slightly. The maximum density, 999.97 kg m−3, is reached at 3.98 °C (Wagner and Pruß 2002).
Water stores a lot of heat. Heating water requires energy to break hydrogen bonds as well as to make the molecules move faster. The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of liquid water by 1 °C at 25 °C is 4.18 J (International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam 2011), several times more than for most common liquids and solids. Oceans and lakes therefore change temperature slowly.

Key points

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom in a bond attracts the shared electrons. On the Pauling scale: H 2.20, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44, P 2.19. It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Unequal sharing makes a bond polar, with partial charges \(\delta\)+ and \(\delta\)−. O–H and N–H bonds are strongly polar; C–H bonds nearly non-polar.
A molecule is polar if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Bent water (1.857 D) is polar; straight CO2 and symmetric CH4 are not.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent bonds: dipole-dipole forces, dispersion forces and, strongest, hydrogen bonds.
A hydrogen bond X–H···Y links a hydrogen on oxygen or nitrogen to a lone pair on another oxygen or nitrogen. It is directional and easily broken.
Hydrogen bonding explains why water boils at 100 °C while methane, of similar mass, boils at −162 °C.
Water dissolves polar molecules by hydrogen bonding and ions by weakening the force between them (relative permittivity 78.4) and forming hydration shells. Like dissolves like.
Non-polar molecules cluster in water (the hydrophobic effect). Amphiphilic molecules form layers and membranes.
Ice is less dense than liquid water and floats; liquid water is densest at 3.98 °C and has a high heat capacity.

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
The question of this chapter
A chemist who wants to make water from hydrogen and oxygen needs two molecules of hydrogen for every molecule of oxygen. Molecules, however, cannot be counted one by one; even a speck of matter contains far too many. This chapter asks: how do chemists count molecules? The answer is the mole, a unit that links the number of particles to a mass that can be weighed. From it follow the molar mass, the concentration of a solution, and the behaviour of gases.
crumbs: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
6.1 The mole

Counting by weighing
A bank that receives a large bag of identical coins does not count them one by one; it weighs them. If one coin has a mass of 5.00 g and the bag contains 2.50 kg of coins, the bag holds 500 coins. Chemists count atoms and molecules in the same way: the mass of a sample, divided by the mass of one particle, gives the number of particles. The only difficulty is that the numbers are enormous, and a special unit is used to handle them.


Definition of the mole
The mole (symbol mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. Since 2019 it has been defined by fixing the number of particles it contains: one mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 × 1023 specified elementary entities (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures 2019). The entities may be atoms, molecules, ions or electrons, and they must always be stated: one mole of water molecules, one mole of sodium ions. The fixed number, expressed per mole, is the Avogadro constant:
\[
N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022\,140\,76 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol}^{-1}
\]
It is exact by definition (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). The amount of substance n and the number of particles N are related by
\[
N = n \times N_\mathrm{A}
\]
Two moles of hydrogen molecules therefore contain 2 × 6.022 × 1023 = 1.204 × 1024 molecules.
The mole is a counting unit, like a dozen, but for a number with 24 digits. Its size was chosen for convenience. Before 2019 the mole was defined by requiring the molar mass of carbon-12 to be exactly 12 g per mole, so that the Avogadro constant was the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12 (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, n.d.). The new definition was chosen to agree with the old one within the precision of measurement. As a result, one mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to the relative mass of its molecules, introduced in Chapter 2. This is what makes the mole so useful.
crumbs: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
6.2 Molar mass

From daltons to grams per mole
The molar mass of a substance, symbol M, is the mass of one mole of it, usually given in grams per mole (g mol−1). Numerically, the molar mass in g mol−1 equals the relative molecular mass (or the atomic weight, for an element). A water molecule has a relative molecular mass of 18.015 (Chapter 2), so the molar mass of water is 18.015 g mol−1: one mole of water, 6.022 × 1023 molecules, has a mass of 18.015 g, a little more than a tablespoon of water.
The molar mass of a compound is calculated by adding the atomic weights of its atoms. For carbon dioxide, CO2:
\[
M(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 12.011 + 2 \times 15.999 = 44.009\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}
\]
For ribose, C5H10O5 (Chapter 4):
\[
M = 5 \times 12.011 + 10 \times 1.0080 + 5 \times 15.999 = 150.13\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}
\]


Converting between mass, amount and number
The amount of substance in a sample of mass m is
\[
n = \frac{m}{M}
\]
and the number of particles follows by multiplying by NA. Chapter 1 stated that a drop of water of about 0.05 mL contains about 1.7 × 1021 water molecules. The calculation runs as follows. Water at room temperature has a density of 997 kg m−3 (International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam 2011), very nearly 1 g per millilitre, so the drop has a mass of about 0.050 g. Its amount of substance is
\[
n = \frac{0.050\ \mathrm{g}}{18.015\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}
\]
and the number of molecules is 2.8 × 10−3 mol × 6.022 × 1023 mol−1 = 1.7 × 1021.
The same steps run in reverse. To prepare 0.10 mol of sodium chloride (molar mass 22.990 + 35.45 = 58.44 g mol−1), weigh out 0.10 × 58.44 = 5.8 g.


How small a molecule is
The Avogadro constant also gives the mass of a single molecule. One water molecule has a mass of 18.015 g mol−1 divided by 6.022 × 1023 mol−1, which is 2.99 × 10−23 g. Since each molecule in liquid water occupies a volume equal to the molar volume divided by NA, and one mole of liquid water occupies about 18 mL, each molecule has about 3.0 × 10−23 mL, or 3.0 × 10−29 m3, to itself: the volume of a cube about 0.31 nm on each side. A water molecule is therefore a few tenths of a nanometre across.
crumbs: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
6.3 Concentration

Amount concentration
Most of the chemistry of life takes place in water. To describe a solution, it is not enough to know how much solute it contains; what matters is how much solute there is in a given volume. The amount concentration, often simply called the concentration, is the amount of solute divided by the volume of the solution:
\[
c = \frac{n}{V}
\]
It is usually expressed in moles per litre (mol L−1), a unit written M and called “molar”. A solution containing 0.10 mol of sodium chloride in a total volume of 1.0 L has a concentration of 0.10 mol L−1, or 0.10 M. The concentration of a substance X is often written [X], so that this statement can be written [NaCl] = 0.10 M.
Concentrations in the chemistry of life span many orders of magnitude, and the SI prefixes are used: millimolar (mM, 10−3 M), micromolar (\(\mu\)M, 10−6 M) and nanomolar (nM, 10−9 M).


Some concentrations for orientation

Pure water. One litre of water at 25 °C has a mass of 997 g, which is 997/18.015 = 55.3 mol. The “concentration” of water in water is therefore about 55 M. This large number reappears whenever water takes part in a reaction.
Sea water. In the standard composition of present-day sea water, the main dissolved ions are chloride (0.546 mol per kilogram of sea water), sodium (0.469 mol kg−1), magnesium (0.0528 mol kg−1) and sulfate (0.0282 mol kg−1) (Millero et al. 2008). Sea water is therefore roughly half a mole per litre in sodium chloride.
Dilute building blocks. Many experiments on the origin of life use the starting materials at millimolar concentrations or higher. Natural waters on the early Earth may have contained some of these molecules at much lower concentrations, and how they could have been concentrated is one of the central questions of the field.

Figure 6.1 places these concentrations on a logarithmic scale.






Figure 6.1: Concentrations on a logarithmic scale, from pure water (about 55 M) to 1 nM, with the corresponding average number of molecules in a volume of 1 \(\mu\)m3 (10−15 L), calculated as c × V × NA. The sea-water value is for chloride (Millero et al. 2008).



Concentrations are sometimes given in units of mass instead of amount, such as grams per litre (g L−1) or milligrams per litre. To convert a mass concentration into an amount concentration, divide by the molar mass: 9.0 g L−1 of sodium chloride is 9.0/58.44 = 0.15 M.


Concentration and the number of molecules in a small volume
At low concentrations and in small volumes, the number of molecules can become very small. A volume of 1 \(\mu\)m3, a cube one micrometre on each side, is 10−15 L. At a concentration of 1 nM it contains
\[
10^{-9}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}} \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{L} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = 0.6
\]
molecules on average, that is, sometimes none and sometimes one or two. A bacterial cell is about this size. Inside it, “1 nanomolar” therefore means roughly one molecule per cell, and any notion of a smoothly varying concentration breaks down.
crumbs: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
6.4 Dilution and concentration

Dilution
Adding solvent to a solution does not change the amount of solute it contains; it only spreads the solute through a larger volume. Since n = cV is the same before and after,
\[
c_1 V_1 = c_2 V_2
\]
where c1 and V1 are the concentration and volume before dilution, and c2 and V2 after. Diluting 10 mL of a 1.0 M solution to 100 mL gives a concentration of 1.0 M × 10 mL / 100 mL = 0.10 M, a tenfold dilution.


Concentration by evaporation
The same equation, read in the other direction, describes concentration. If water evaporates from a solution and the solute stays behind, the volume falls and the concentration rises in proportion. A pond that loses 99 % of its water by evaporation concentrates every non-volatile solute a hundredfold, provided that nothing is lost by other routes, such as crystallisation, seepage or reaction. Repeated drying and wetting of shallow pools is one of the main mechanisms proposed for concentrating the building blocks of life on the early Earth, and the arithmetic of concentration is simply the dilution equation run backwards.
crumbs: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration

title: 6  Counting Molecules: Moles and Concentration
text:
6.5 Gases

The ideal gas law
In a gas, the molecules are far apart and move independently. For most gases near ordinary temperatures and pressures, pressure p, volume V, amount n and absolute temperature T are related by the ideal gas law:
\[
pV = nRT
\]
where R is the molar gas constant, 8.314 J mol−1 K−1 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). Its value is exact, since it is the product of two constants fixed by definition, the Avogadro constant and the Boltzmann constant. Pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the gas on the walls of its container, measured in pascals (Pa); the bar, equal to 105 Pa, is close to atmospheric pressure at sea level, and the standard atmosphere is exactly 101 325 Pa.
The ideal gas law contains a remarkable fact: the volume of a gas depends on the number of its molecules, not on what they are. At 25 °C (298.15 K) and 1 bar, one mole of any ideal gas occupies
\[
V = \frac{nRT}{p} = \frac{1\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}} \times 298.15\ \mathrm{K}}{10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}} = 0.0248\ \mathrm{m^3} = 24.8\ \mathrm{L}
\]


Mixtures of gases and partial pressure
In a mixture of gases, each gas contributes to the total pressure in proportion to its amount. The pressure that a gas in a mixture would exert if it alone filled the container is its partial pressure, and the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. The partial pressure of each gas equals its fraction of the molecules multiplied by the total pressure.
Dry air today consists, by volume and therefore by number of molecules, of 78.08 % nitrogen, 20.95 % oxygen and 0.93 % argon, together with smaller amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases (NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive 2024). At a total pressure of 1 bar, the partial pressure of oxygen is therefore about 0.21 bar. The atmosphere of the early Earth was very different: it contained essentially no free oxygen, and its composition is one of the main uncertainties in the study of the origin of life.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
The question of this chapter
When methane burns, it disappears, and carbon dioxide and water appear in its place. When iron rusts, a grey metal becomes a red-brown powder. In every such change, atoms are neither created nor destroyed; they are only rearranged into new combinations. This chapter asks: how is a chemical reaction described, and what kinds of reaction are there? It shows how reactions are written as balanced equations, how the amounts of substances in a reaction are calculated, and how most reactions in the chemistry of life fall into a few types: transfers of protons, transfers of electrons, and the joining and splitting of molecules with water.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.1 What happens in a reaction

Reactants and products
A chemical reaction is a process in which substances are converted into different substances by the breaking and forming of chemical bonds. The substances present at the start are the reactants, and those formed are the products. In the burning of methane, the reactants are methane and oxygen and the products are carbon dioxide and water. The C–H bonds of methane and the O=O bonds of oxygen are broken, and new C=O and O–H bonds are formed.
A chemical reaction changes only the arrangement of electrons and the way atoms are bonded together. The nuclei are untouched, so every atom present among the reactants is still present among the products, as an atom of the same element. This distinguishes chemical reactions from the nuclear reactions of stars and radioactive decay, which change one element into another.


Conservation of mass
Because atoms are only rearranged, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. This law of conservation of mass was established by careful weighing in the late eighteenth century, most influentially by Antoine Lavoisier (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.). It holds to the precision of any chemical balance. (According to relativity, the energy released in a reaction corresponds to a tiny loss of mass, but for chemical reactions it is far too small to measure by weighing.)

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.2 Chemical equations

Writing an equation
A reaction is written as a chemical equation, with the formulas of the reactants on the left, the formulas of the products on the right, and an arrow between them pointing from reactants to products. The formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen is written
\[
2\,\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}
\]
The numbers in front of the formulas are called coefficients. They give the number of molecules (or moles) of each substance that take part. A coefficient of 1 is not written. The equation reads: two molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of oxygen to give two molecules of water (Figure 7.1).






Figure 7.1: The reaction 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O drawn as molecules. Hydrogen atoms are grey and oxygen atoms red. The left side contains four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms, and so does the right side: the equation is balanced.





Balancing an equation
An equation is balanced when each side contains the same number of atoms of every element, and the same total charge. To balance an equation, change only the coefficients, never the subscripts in the formulas: changing a subscript would describe a different substance. The usual procedure is to balance first the elements that appear in only one substance on each side, and to leave hydrogen and oxygen, which often appear in several, until last.
As an example, consider the burning of methane. The unbalanced equation is
\[
\mathrm{CH_4} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}
\]
Carbon is already balanced, with one atom on each side. Methane supplies four hydrogen atoms, so two molecules of water are needed: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O. The right side now contains 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, so two molecules of oxygen are needed on the left:
\[
\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}
\]
A final count confirms one carbon, four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms on each side.
Equations involving ions must also balance charge. In the reaction of sodium with chlorine to give ions, Na + Cl → Na+ + Cl−, the total charge is zero on both sides.


State symbols
The physical state of each substance is often added in parentheses after its formula: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid, (g) for gas and (aq) for a substance dissolved in water (from the Latin aqua). Dissolving table salt is written
\[
\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}
\]


Arrows
Different arrows have different meanings, and they must not be confused.

A single arrow, →, shows the direction of a reaction from reactants to products.
A pair of half-arrows, \(\rightleftharpoons\), shows a reversible reaction: one that proceeds in both directions at once, and in which reactants and products coexist. Such a reaction reaches a state of balance, called equilibrium, described in Chapter 8. Strictly, every reaction is reversible; the single arrow is used when the reverse reaction is negligible.
A double-headed arrow, \(\leftrightarrow\), does not denote a reaction at all. It connects two resonance structures of the same molecule (Chapter 4).
Curved arrows, drawn on structures, show the movement of pairs of electrons during a reaction. They are used to describe reaction mechanisms, the step-by-step paths by which reactions occur (Chapter 11).

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.3 Amounts in reactions

Coefficients are ratios of moles
The coefficients of a balanced equation give the ratios in which molecules react. Since a mole is a fixed number of molecules (Chapter 6), they also give the ratios in moles. The equation CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O states that one mole of methane reacts with two moles of oxygen to give one mole of carbon dioxide and two moles of water. The calculation of amounts of reactants and products from a balanced equation is called stoichiometry (from the Greek stoicheion, element, and metron, measure).


A worked example
How much carbon dioxide and water are produced when 16.0 g of methane burns completely? The molar mass of methane is 12.011 + 4 × 1.0080 = 16.04 g mol−1, so 16.0 g is 0.998 mol, very nearly one mole. By the equation, this gives 0.998 mol of CO2 and 2 × 0.998 = 2.00 mol of H2O. With molar masses of 44.01 and 18.015 g mol−1, these are 43.9 g of carbon dioxide and 36.0 g of water.
The masses confirm conservation of mass. The reactants are 16.0 g of methane and 2 × 0.998 mol × 32.00 g mol−1 = 63.9 g of oxygen, a total of 79.9 g. The products are 43.9 g + 36.0 g = 79.9 g.


The limiting reactant
Reactants are rarely mixed in exactly the ratio of the equation. The reactant that runs out first is the limiting reactant; it determines how much product is formed, and the others are left over in excess. If 1 mol of methane is burned with only 1 mol of oxygen, oxygen is limiting: it can react with only 0.5 mol of methane, giving 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide and 1 mol of water, and 0.5 mol of methane remains. In the chemistry of the origin of life, the scarcest reactant, whether phosphate, a particular sugar or an energy-rich compound, often limits how much of a product can form, however abundant the others may be.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.4 Transferring protons: acids and bases
Many reactions in water involve the transfer of a single proton, that is, a hydrogen ion H+, which is a hydrogen atom without its electron. An acid is a substance that donates a proton, and a base is a substance that accepts one. When hydrogen chloride dissolves in water, it donates its proton to a water molecule:
\[
\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}
\]
Here HCl is the acid and water is the base. The ion H3O+, a water molecule carrying an extra proton, is the hydronium ion. When ammonia dissolves in water, water acts as the acid and ammonia as the base:
\[
\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{OH^-}
\]
The products are the ammonium ion and the hydroxide ion. Water can act either as an acid or as a base, depending on its partner. Proton transfers are among the fastest of all reactions, and the balance between acids and bases in a solution is measured by its pH. Both are the subject of Chapter 8.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.5 Transferring electrons: oxidation and reduction

Definitions
A second large class of reactions involves the transfer of electrons. Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule, and reduction is the gain of electrons. The two always occur together, because electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another, and the combined process is called a redox reaction (from reduction and oxidation). The substance that gains electrons, and so causes the oxidation of its partner, is the oxidising agent; the substance that loses electrons is the reducing agent.
The reaction of sodium with chlorine is a redox reaction: each sodium atom loses an electron (it is oxidised) and each chlorine atom gains one (it is reduced). Another example, important in the geochemistry of the early Earth, is the oxidation of dissolved iron(II) ions, Fe2+, to iron(III), Fe3+, each by loss of one electron. Oxygen is a strong oxidising agent, and the word oxidation originally meant combination with oxygen; but many oxidations involve no oxygen at all.


Oxidation numbers
In reactions between molecules, electrons are often not transferred completely but shifted partly from one atom towards another. To keep track of such shifts, each atom is assigned an oxidation number (or oxidation state): the charge it would have if all its bonds were fully ionic, with the shared electrons of each bond given to the more electronegative atom (Chapter 5). For most purposes a few rules are enough.

An atom in an element (H2, O2, N2, C as graphite) has oxidation number 0.
Hydrogen bonded to a more electronegative atom, as in all compounds in this book, has +1. Oxygen usually has −2.
The oxidation numbers of the atoms in a molecule add up to its charge: zero for a neutral molecule, and the charge of the ion for an ion.

An increase in oxidation number is oxidation, and a decrease is reduction.


A ladder of carbon compounds
The rules show that carbon can exist at many levels of oxidation. In methane, CH4, each hydrogen is +1, so carbon is −4. In methanol, CH3OH, three hydrogens on carbon (+3 in total), one oxygen (−2) and one hydrogen on oxygen (+1) leave carbon at −2. Continuing in this way gives the ladder of Figure 7.2: methane (−4), methanol (−2), formaldehyde, H2CO (0), formic acid, HCOOH (+2), and carbon dioxide, CO2 (+4). Each step up the ladder is an oxidation by two electrons, and each step down a reduction.






Figure 7.2: Oxidation numbers of carbon in five one-carbon compounds. Moving to the right, each step removes two electrons from carbon (oxidation); moving to the left adds two electrons (reduction). Carbon dioxide is the most oxidised form of carbon, methane the most reduced.



This ladder matters for the origin of life. The carbon of living matter lies mostly in the middle of the ladder, at oxidation numbers between −2 and +2, as in sugars, whose carbon atoms average 0. On the early Earth, much of the carbon was present as carbon dioxide, at the top. Making the building blocks of life from carbon dioxide therefore requires reduction: a supply of electrons from a reducing agent, such as hydrogen gas, iron(II) or the energy of sunlight. Whether the early atmosphere and oceans were reducing (rich in electron donors) or more oxidised is one of the long-standing questions of the field.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
7.6 Joining and splitting with water

Condensation
A third type of reaction is central to the chemistry of life. In a condensation reaction, two molecules join to form a larger molecule, and a small molecule, usually water, is released. The reaction of an acid with an alcohol to form a compound called an ester is an example (Figure 7.3):
\[
\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COOCH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}
\]
An OH group from the acid and an H atom from the alcohol leave together as water, and a new bond joins the remaining parts. The product, ethyl acetate, is an ester; Chapter 11 describes this and other groups formed by condensation.






Figure 7.3: Condensation and hydrolysis. Acetic acid and ethanol combine to form the ester ethyl acetate, releasing a molecule of water (condensation, forward direction). Adding water splits the ester back into the acid and the alcohol (hydrolysis, reverse direction). The atoms that form the water are highlighted.



The large molecules of life are all built by condensation. Proteins are chains of amino acids, each joined to the next by a condensation that releases water. RNA and DNA are chains of nucleotides, joined by condensations between phosphate groups and the hydroxy groups of sugars. Even the attachment of a nucleobase to a sugar is a condensation.


Hydrolysis
The reverse of condensation is hydrolysis (from the Greek for “splitting by water”): a reaction in which water breaks a bond, its H going to one fragment and its OH to the other. Ethyl acetate is hydrolysed back to acetic acid and ethanol; proteins are hydrolysed to amino acids, and RNA to its nucleotides.
Condensation and hydrolysis are a reversible pair, and in water, where water molecules are present at about 55 mol L−1 (Chapter 6), the balance usually lies on the side of hydrolysis. A chain of RNA dissolved in water is therefore always at risk of being cut by hydrolysis, and its building blocks do not join of their own accord. How chains could nevertheless have formed in water on the early Earth is one of the central problems of the origin of life. Chapters 8 and 9 explain why the large amount of water favours hydrolysis, and Chapter 12 returns to the question.


Addition
In an addition reaction, two molecules combine to form a single product, and no small molecule is released. Additions to double bonds are common. Water can add to the C=O double bond of formaldehyde, and hydrogen cyanide can add to it to form a larger molecule containing two carbon atoms:
\[
\mathrm{HCN} + \mathrm{H_2CO} \rightarrow \mathrm{HOCH_2CN}
\]
Additions of this kind, which build new carbon-carbon bonds from small molecules such as hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde, are thought to be among the first steps by which more complex organic molecules formed on the early Earth.

title: 7  Chemical Reactions and Equations
text:
Key points

A chemical reaction rearranges atoms by breaking and forming bonds; atoms of each element are conserved, and so is mass.
A chemical equation lists reactants, an arrow, and products, with coefficients giving the number of molecules or moles. A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element, and the same charge, on both sides.
→ marks a reaction, \(\rightleftharpoons\) a reversible reaction, \(\leftrightarrow\) resonance (not a reaction). State symbols are (s), (l), (g), (aq).
Coefficients are mole ratios. Stoichiometry converts between masses and amounts: 16 g of methane burns to 44 g of CO2 and 36 g of water. The limiting reactant determines the yield.
Acid-base reactions transfer protons (H+). An acid donates a proton and a base accepts one; water can act as either.
Redox reactions transfer electrons: oxidation is loss, reduction gain. Oxidation numbers track the shifts; carbon ranges from −4 in CH4 to +4 in CO2. Making biological molecules from CO2 requires reduction.
Condensation joins two molecules and releases water; hydrolysis is the reverse. Proteins, RNA and DNA are built by condensation and broken by hydrolysis, which water favours.
In an addition reaction, two molecules combine without losing any atoms.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
The question of this chapter
Many reactions do not go to completion. They stop partway, with reactants and products both present, and nothing further seems to happen however long one waits. This chapter asks: where does a reaction stop, and why? The answer is chemical equilibrium, a balance between a reaction and its reverse that can be described by a single number, the equilibrium constant. The same idea explains what acids and bases do in water, what pH measures, and why the joining of building blocks into chains is so difficult in dilute solution.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.1 Dynamic equilibrium

Two reactions at once
Consider a reversible reaction, A \(\rightleftharpoons\) B. When A is first dissolved, only the forward reaction, A → B, can occur, and B begins to accumulate. As soon as some B is present, the reverse reaction, B → A, also begins. As A is used up, the forward reaction slows; as B accumulates, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually the two rates become equal. From then on, A is converted into B exactly as fast as B is converted back into A, and the amounts of both stay constant (Figure 8.1).
This state is called chemical equilibrium. It is a dynamic equilibrium: at the level of molecules, both reactions continue without pause, but their effects cancel, and nothing changes on the scale of the whole sample. The same final state is reached whether one starts with pure A, pure B, or any mixture of the two, provided that the temperature and the total amounts are the same.






Figure 8.1: Approach to equilibrium for a reaction A \(\rightleftharpoons\) B, starting from pure A. Left: concentrations of A (teal) and B (orange) against time; both level off at their equilibrium values. Right: rates of the forward (A → B) and reverse (B → A) reactions, which become equal at equilibrium. The curves are calculated for a forward rate constant twice as large as the reverse one, so that at equilibrium [B] = 2[A].





Equilibrium is not equality
Equilibrium does not mean that reactants and products are present in equal amounts. It means that their amounts no longer change. In some reactions, the equilibrium mixture contains almost nothing but products; in others, almost nothing but reactants; and in many, appreciable amounts of both. Which of these applies is expressed by the equilibrium constant.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.2 The equilibrium constant

Definition
For a reaction written in general form as
\[
a\,\mathrm{A} + b\,\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\,\mathrm{C} + d\,\mathrm{D}
\]
where the lower-case letters are the coefficients, the equilibrium constant K is
\[
K = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{c}\,[\mathrm{D}]^{d}}{[\mathrm{A}]^{a}\,[\mathrm{B}]^{b}}
\]
where the square brackets denote the concentrations at equilibrium. The products appear in the numerator and the reactants in the denominator, each raised to the power of its coefficient. At a given temperature, K has a fixed value for each reaction, whatever the starting amounts.
Two conventions make K a pure number and keep it simple. First, each concentration is divided by a standard concentration of 1 mol L−1, so that [A] stands for the number of moles per litre without the unit. Strictly, K is defined with activities, effective concentrations that allow for the interactions between dissolved particles, but in dilute solutions activities are close to concentrations divided by 1 mol L−1. Second, pure solids and pure liquids, and the solvent of a dilute solution, have activities of 1 and are left out of the expression. In reactions in dilute aqueous solution, water therefore does not appear in K, even when it is a reactant or a product.


What the size of K means

If K is much larger than 1, the numerator dominates at equilibrium: the reaction lies far to the right, and the equilibrium mixture consists mostly of products.
If K is much smaller than 1, the reaction lies far to the left, and little product forms.
If K is close to 1, appreciable amounts of both reactants and products are present.

Because equilibrium constants range over many orders of magnitude, from 10−30 or less to 1030 or more, they are often given as logarithms, in the form pK = −log10 K, which turns the range into a manageable span of numbers. This is the origin of the “p” in pH and pKa, described below.


An important consequence: dilution and joining
The concentrations in K are raised to powers, and this has a consequence that runs through the whole chemistry of the origin of life. Consider a condensation in water, in which two building blocks A and B join to form AB and release water:
\[
\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{AB} + \mathrm{H_2O}
\]
Since water is the solvent, it does not appear in K, and
\[
K = \frac{[\mathrm{AB}]}{[\mathrm{A}]\,[\mathrm{B}]}, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \frac{[\mathrm{AB}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = K \times [\mathrm{B}]
\]
The fraction of A that is joined to B depends not only on K but also on the concentration of B. Suppose, for example, that K = 10. If B is present at 1 mol L−1, then [AB]/[A] = 10: most of A is joined. If B is present at 1 mM, then [AB]/[A] = 10 × 0.001 = 0.01: only about 1 % of A is joined. At 1 \(\mu\)M, only about one A in 100 000. The more dilute the solution, the more the equilibrium favours the separate building blocks and the less it favours the joined product. Dilute solutions favour hydrolysis.
This simple relation explains why the chains of life do not form spontaneously from dilute building blocks in water, and why so much attention is paid to ways of concentrating them, by evaporation, freezing or adsorption on mineral surfaces, and of removing water, by drying.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.3 Shifting an equilibrium

Le Chatelier’s principle
An equilibrium can be disturbed by changing the conditions: adding or removing a reactant or product, changing the temperature, or, for gases, changing the pressure. The response follows a general rule known as Le Chatelier’s principle: when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance.

Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, consuming some of the added reactant and forming more product. Removing a product has the same effect. A reaction whose product is continually removed, for example because it crystallises out of solution or escapes as a gas, can be driven almost to completion even if its K is small.
Removing water from a condensation, A + B \(\rightleftharpoons\) AB + H2O, shifts it towards AB. In dilute solution the water is the solvent and cannot be removed without concentrating everything else; but when a solution is dried, water is no longer present in excess, its activity falls below 1, and condensation becomes more favourable. This is one reason why wet-dry cycles are thought to have helped build chains on the early Earth.
Changing the temperature changes the value of K itself. Raising the temperature favours the direction that absorbs heat. Chapter 9 explains why.

Adding a catalyst, a substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed (Chapter 10), does not shift an equilibrium at all. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so that equilibrium is reached sooner, but the equilibrium mixture is the same.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.4 Water, acids and bases

Water ionises itself
Water itself takes part in an equilibrium. A small fraction of water molecules transfer a proton to a neighbouring water molecule:
\[
2\,\mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{OH^-}
\]
Because water is the solvent, its activity is 1, and the equilibrium constant reduces to the product of the activities of the two ions. This constant is the ion product of water, Kw. At 25 °C, pKw = −log10 Kw = 13.99 (International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam 2024), so Kw = 1.0 × 10−14. In pure water the two ions are present in equal amounts, each at a concentration of about 10−7 mol L−1. Since pure water contains about 55 mol L−1 of water molecules (Chapter 6), only about two molecules in a thousand million are ionised at any moment.


pH
The concentration of hydronium ions in a solution determines its acidity. Because this concentration varies over many orders of magnitude, it is expressed on a logarithmic scale (Chapter 1). The pH of a solution is defined as
\[
\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10} a(\mathrm{H_3O^+})
\]
where a(H3O+) is the activity of the hydronium ion, which in dilute solution is close to its concentration in mol L−1. A solution with [H3O+] = 10−7 M has pH 7; one with 10−3 M has pH 3. Each unit of pH is a factor of ten, so a solution of pH 3 contains ten thousand times as many hydronium ions as a solution of pH 7.
Since the activities of H3O+ and OH− multiply to Kw, an increase in one means a decrease in the other. A solution is neutral when the two are equal, which at 25 °C is at pH 7.00. A solution with a lower pH is acidic, and one with a higher pH is basic (or alkaline). Figure 8.2 shows the scale.






Figure 8.2: The pH scale at 25 °C. Each step of one unit is a factor of ten in the concentration of hydronium ions (top) and, in the opposite direction, of hydroxide ions (bottom). Pure water is neutral at pH 7; the fluids of the Lost City hydrothermal field have pH 9 to 11 (Kelley et al. 2005).





Neutral is not always pH 7
The value of Kw depends strongly on temperature, and so does the pH of neutral water (Table 8.1). At 0 °C neutral water has pH 7.48, and at 100 °C it has pH 6.13. A hot spring at 100 °C with pH 6.5 is therefore slightly basic, not acidic. This matters when comparing the waters of cold pools, hot springs and hydrothermal vents, all of which have been proposed as settings for the origin of life.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.5 Strong and weak acids

Strong acids
An acid is a proton donor (Chapter 7). A strong acid, such as hydrochloric acid, gives up its proton to water essentially completely; in its solution, no undissociated HCl molecules remain. A 0.01 M solution of hydrochloric acid therefore contains 0.01 M H3O+ and has pH 2.


Weak acids and Ka
Most acids in the chemistry of life are weak acids: they donate their protons only partly, and an equilibrium is established between the acid and its deprotonated form. For a weak acid HA,
\[
\mathrm{HA} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{A^-}
\]
The species A− that remains after HA has lost its proton is called the conjugate base of HA. The equilibrium constant of this reaction, with water omitted, is the acid dissociation constant:
\[
K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\,[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}
\]
and it is usually given as pKa = −log10 Ka. The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid. Acetic acid, the acid of vinegar, has pKa = 4.76 (Goldberg et al. 2002).


pH and pKa: which form is present?
Taking logarithms of the expression for Ka gives a simple and very useful relation between the pH and the ratio of the two forms of an acid:
\[
\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} + \log_{10}\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}
\]
It is known as the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, and its consequences can be read off directly.

When pH = pKa, the logarithm is zero, so [A−] = [HA]: the acid is half dissociated.
For each unit of pH above the pKa, the ratio [A−]/[HA] increases tenfold. Two units above the pKa, the acid is 99 % in its deprotonated form, A−.
For each unit below, the ratio decreases tenfold. Two units below, the acid is 99 % in its protonated form, HA.

At pH 7, acetic acid, with pKa = 4.76, is more than 99 % in the form of the acetate ion, CH3COO−. The carboxy groups of amino acids and other biological acids are likewise almost entirely deprotonated, and negatively charged, at neutral pH.


Phosphoric acid and phosphate
Phosphoric acid, H3PO4, has three O–H groups, each of which can lose a proton, with three successive pKa values of about 2.1, 7.2 and 12.4 (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.). Depending on the pH, it is present as H3PO4, H2PO4−, HPO42− or PO43− (Figure 8.3). Near pH 7, H2PO4− and HPO42− are present in similar amounts. The general word phosphate covers all these forms.






Figure 8.3: Fraction of phosphate present in each of its four forms as a function of pH, calculated from the three pKa values 2.14, 7.20 and 12.37 (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.). Each crossing point, where two forms are present in equal amounts, lies at a pKa.



In RNA, each phosphate group is joined to two sugars and keeps only one O–H group of its own. This remaining group is a strong acid, much stronger than the second O–H group of phosphoric acid, and at neutral pH it has lost its proton: each phosphate linkage of an RNA chain carries one negative charge (Westheimer 1987). An RNA chain of 100 nucleotides carries about 100 negative charges along its backbone.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
8.6 Buffers
A solution that contains a weak acid together with its conjugate base, in comparable amounts, resists changes in pH. Such a solution is called a buffer. If a strong acid is added, the added H3O+ ions are largely taken up by A−, forming HA; if a strong base is added, the OH− ions are largely neutralised by HA, forming A− and water. In either case the ratio [A−]/[HA] changes only a little, and by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation the pH changes only a little.
A buffer works best when the pH is close to the pKa of its acid, where the two forms are present in similar amounts. A mixture of H2PO4− and HPO42−, with pKa = 7.2, buffers near neutral pH, and phosphate buffers are among the most widely used in laboratories. Natural waters are also buffered, mainly by dissolved carbon dioxide and its ions, and by reactions with minerals. Laboratory experiments on the origin of life are usually run in buffered solutions, so that the pH stays where the experimenter has set it; on the early Earth, the pH of each setting would have been set by its own buffers.

title: 8  Equilibrium, Acids and pH
text:
Key points

A reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium when its forward and reverse rates are equal; the amounts then stay constant, though both reactions continue.
For aA + bB \(\rightleftharpoons\) cC + dD, K = [C]c[D]d / ([A]a[B]b), with concentrations in mol L−1 (strictly, activities). Pure solids, pure liquids and the solvent are left out. K \(\gg\) 1 favours products; K \(\ll\) 1 favours reactants.
For a condensation A + B \(\rightleftharpoons\) AB + H2O in water, [AB]/[A] = K[B]: dilution strongly favours the separate building blocks.
Le Chatelier’s principle: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to counteract the disturbance. Removing a product or water drives a reaction forward. A catalyst does not shift an equilibrium.
Water ionises: Kw = 1.0 × 10−14 at 25 °C. pH = −log10 a(H3O+). Neutral water has pH 7.00 at 25 °C, 7.48 at 0 °C and 6.13 at 100 °C.
Strong acids dissociate completely; weak acids partly, with Ka and pKa. pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]). At pH = pKa the acid is half dissociated.
Phosphoric acid has pKa values of about 2.1, 7.2 and 12.4. Each phosphate linkage of RNA carries one negative charge at neutral pH.
A buffer, a weak acid with its conjugate base, resists changes in pH, best near its pKa.
