title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
This glossary lists the technical terms defined in the book, in alphabetical order. Each entry gives the term, its definition, and the chapter in which it is first defined.



Table A.1: Glossary of terms.










Term
Definition
Chapter




Acid
A substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance.
7


Acid dissociation constant (Ka)
The equilibrium constant for the reaction of a weak acid with water, Ka = [H3O+][A−]/[HA]; usually given as pKa = −log10 Ka.
8


Acidic
Describing a solution with a pH below that of neutral water.
8


Activated
Of a molecule: carrying a built-in source of Gibbs energy that can drive a coupled reaction.
9


Activation energy
Ea; the energy that reactants must acquire to reach the transition state.
10


Activity
The effective concentration of a dissolved species, corrected for interactions between particles, expressed relative to a standard concentration of 1 mol L−1.
8


Addition reaction
A reaction in which two molecules combine to form a single product without the loss of any atoms.
7


Alcohol
A compound with a hydroxy group, –OH, on a carbon atom that forms only single bonds.
11


Aldehyde
A compound in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom, R–CHO.
11


Aldose
A sugar whose carbonyl group is an aldehyde.
11


Alkane
A hydrocarbon with only single bonds between carbon atoms.
11


Alkene
A hydrocarbon with at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
11


Alkyne
A hydrocarbon with at least one carbon-carbon triple bond.
11


Amide
A compound derived from an acid by replacing an –OH with a nitrogen group; in a carboxylic amide, C=O is bonded to N.
11


Amine
A compound with a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more carbon atoms and carrying a lone pair; a base.
11


Amino acid
In biology, a molecule with an amino group, a carboxy group and a side chain on the same carbon atom.
12


Amount concentration
The amount of solute divided by the volume of the solution, usually in mol L−1 (M); often simply called the concentration.
6


Amount of substance (n)
The quantity that counts the number of specified entities in a sample, measured in moles.
6


Amphiphilic
Having a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part, like soap; such molecules form layers and membranes in water.
5


Anion
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom or group of atoms gains electrons.
2


Anomers
The two forms, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), that differ in the arrangement at the carbon atom created when a sugar closes its ring.
11


Antiparallel
Of two paired strands: running in opposite 5\('\)-to-3\('\) directions.
12


Aqueous solution
A solution in which water is the solvent.
5


Aromatic
Describing a flat ring, such as benzene, in which the electrons of the double bonds are spread evenly around the ring, giving unusual stability.
4


Arrhenius equation
k = A e−Ea/RT; the dependence of a rate constant on temperature.
10


Arrhenius plot
A graph of ln k against 1/T, a straight line of slope −Ea/R.
10


Atom
The smallest unit of a chemical element, consisting of a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
2


Atomic number (Z)
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it defines the element.
2


Atomic weight
The average mass of the atoms of an element in a natural sample, relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; also called relative atomic mass. It has no unit.
2


ATP
Adenosine triphosphate, the main activated molecule used by cells to drive unfavourable reactions.
9


Autocatalysis
Catalysis of a reaction by one of its own products.
10


Avogadro constant (NA)
The number of entities per mole, exactly 6.022 140 76 × 1023 mol−1.
6


Backbone
The repeating chain of sugars and phosphates (in nucleic acids) or of amide-linked units (in proteins).
12


Balanced equation
A chemical equation with the same number of atoms of each element, and the same total charge, on both sides.
7


Ball-and-stick model
A model of a molecule in which atoms are spheres and bonds are rods, showing bond angles and three-dimensional arrangement.
4


Bar
A unit of pressure equal to 105 Pa, close to atmospheric pressure at sea level.
6


Base
A substance that accepts a proton (H+) from another substance.
7


Base (of a power)
The number that is multiplied by itself in a power; in 103 the base is 10.
1


Basic
Describing a solution with a pH above that of neutral water; also called alkaline.
8


Benzene
The aromatic compound C6H6, a flat ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom.
4


Boltzmann constant
kB = 1.380 649 × 10−23 J K−1 (exact); relates thermal energy per particle to temperature.
9


Boltzmann factor
e−E/RT; approximately the fraction of molecules with an energy of at least E.
10


Bond enthalpy
The energy needed to break a particular bond in the gas phase, given per mole of bonds.
3


Bond length
The distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms.
3


Bond order
The number of electron pairs shared between two bonded atoms: 1 for a single, 2 for a double, 3 for a triple bond.
3


Buffer
A solution containing a weak acid and its conjugate base, which resists changes in pH.
8


Calorie
An older unit of energy; the thermochemical calorie is exactly 4.184 J.
9


Carbonyl group
A carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom, C=O.
11


Carboxy group
The group –COOH, a carbon atom double-bonded to one oxygen atom and single-bonded to an –OH group.
4


Carboxylic acid
A compound containing the carboxy group, –COOH.
11


Catalyst
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without changing its standard Gibbs energy change.
10


Cation
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom or group of atoms loses electrons.
2


Chemical equation
A representation of a reaction, with the formulas of the reactants on the left, an arrow, and the formulas of the products on the right.
7


Chemical equilibrium
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates are equal, so that the amounts of reactants and products no longer change.
8


Chemical formula
A combination of element symbols and subscript numbers giving the number of atoms of each element in a substance, such as H2O.
2


Chemical reaction
A process in which substances are converted into different substances by the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.
7


Chiral
Not superimposable on its mirror image.
11


Coefficient
A number placed in front of a formula in a chemical equation, giving the number of molecules or moles that take part.
7


Complementary
Of two sequences: able to form Watson–Crick pairs along their whole length.
12


Compound
A pure substance made of two or more elements combined in fixed proportions.
2


Condensation
A reaction in which two molecules join to form a larger molecule, releasing a small molecule, usually water.
7


Condensed formula
A formula that lists atoms in the order in which they are connected, grouping each carbon with its hydrogen atoms, such as CH3CH2OH.
4


Conjugate base
The species that remains when an acid has lost a proton, such as acetate from acetic acid.
8


Conservation of mass
The law that the total mass of the products of a chemical reaction equals the total mass of the reactants.
7


Constitutional isomers
Isomers whose atoms are bonded in a different order.
11


Coupling
Driving an unfavourable reaction by linking it, through a shared intermediate, to a favourable one.
9


Covalent bond
A chemical bond formed by a pair of electrons shared between two atoms.
3


Curved arrow
A symbol showing the movement of an electron pair in a reaction mechanism.
11


D and L
Labels for the two enantiomeric series of sugars and amino acids, based on comparison with glyceraldehyde.
11


Dalton (Da)
The unit of atomic and molecular mass, one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1.660 539 068 92 × 10−27 kg; also called the unified atomic mass unit (u).
2


Dashed bond
In a structural drawing, a bond that points behind the page, away from the viewer.
4


Deoxyribose
The sugar of DNA, ribose lacking the hydroxy group on carbon 2\('\).
12


Derived unit
A unit formed by multiplying or dividing base units, such as the joule, 1 kg m2 s−2.
1


Dipole
A separation of positive and negative charge; a molecule with a dipole has a partially positive and a partially negative end.
5


Dipole moment
A measure of the size of a dipole, usually given in debye (D); water has 1.857 D.
5


Dipole-dipole interaction
The attraction between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another.
5


Dispersion force
A weak attraction between all molecules, caused by temporary fluctuations in their electron clouds; also called the London force.
5


Double bond
A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared.
3


Dynamic equilibrium
An equilibrium in which forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates, so that no net change occurs.
8


e
The base of natural exponentials and logarithms, 2.718 28…; ex is also written exp(x).
1


Electron
A particle with charge −e and mass 9.1094 × 10−31 kg, found outside the nucleus of an atom.
2


Electron configuration
A list of the number of electrons in each subshell of an atom, such as 1s2 2s2 2p2 for carbon.
3


Electronegativity
The tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons towards itself; on the Pauling scale, H 2.20, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44.
5


Electronvolt (eV)
The energy gained by an elementary charge moving through a potential difference of one volt; exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 J.
3


Electrophile
An electron-poor species that forms a bond by accepting both bonding electrons from its partner.
11


Element
A pure substance whose atoms all have the same atomic number; it cannot be broken down by chemical means.
2


Elementary charge (e)
The charge of a proton, exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 C; the electron has charge −e.
2


Enantiomers
Two molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
11


5\('\) end and 3\('\) end
The two ends of a nucleic acid chain; sequences are written from 5\('\) to 3\('\).
12


Endergonic
Having ΔG > 0; unfavourable.
9


Endothermic
Absorbing heat from the surroundings (ΔH > 0).
9


Energy
The capacity to do work or to supply heat; SI unit the joule.
9


Energy level
One of the fixed energies that an electron in an atom can have.
3


Enthalpy
H; its change, ΔH, equals the heat exchanged by a process at constant pressure.
9


Entropy
S; a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the observed state of a system.
9


Enzyme
A biological catalyst, usually a protein.
10


Equilibrium constant (K)
For aA + bB \(\rightleftharpoons\) cC + dD, the ratio [C]c[D]d/([A]a[B]b) at equilibrium, with concentrations relative to 1 mol L−1; fixed at a given temperature.
8


Ester
A compound formed from an acid and an alcohol with the loss of water.
11


Ether
A compound with an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms, C–O–C.
11


Exergonic
Having ΔG < 0; favourable.
9


Exothermic
Releasing heat to the surroundings (ΔH < 0).
9


Exponent
The number that states how many times the base appears as a factor in a power; in 103 the exponent is 3. A negative exponent denotes division.
1


Exponential change
Change by a constant factor in each equal interval of time, so that the elapsed time appears in an exponent.
1


First law of thermodynamics
Energy is conserved: it can be transferred and converted but not created or destroyed.
9


First-order reaction
A reaction whose rate is proportional to the concentration of one reactant.
10


Fischer projection
A drawing convention for chains of stereocentres: vertical bonds point away from the viewer, horizontal bonds towards.
11


Formal charge
A charge assigned to an individual atom in a structure, such as O− with one bond or N+ with four.
4


Functional group
A group of atoms that gives a molecule characteristic properties and reactions, largely independent of the rest of the molecule.
11


Furanose
The five-membered ring form of a sugar (four carbons and one oxygen).
11


Gas
A state of matter in which particles are far apart and move freely, so that the substance fills its container.
2


Gibbs energy
G = H − TS; at constant temperature and pressure a change is spontaneous only if ΔG < 0.
9


Ground state
The lowest-energy, most stable state of an atom or molecule.
3


Group (periodic table)
A column of the periodic table; elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemistry.
2


Half-life (t1/2)
The time in which a quantity that decays exponentially falls to half its value; t1/2 = ln 2 / k.
1


Haworth projection
A drawing of a sugar ring seen obliquely, with the near edge drawn thick and groups placed above or below the plane of the ring.
4


Heat
Energy transferred from one body to another because of a difference in temperature.
9


Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
The relation pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]) between pH and the ratio of the two forms of a weak acid.
8


Hess’s law
The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever the path, and can be calculated from enthalpies of formation.
9


Heterocycle
A ring containing at least one atom other than carbon, such as oxygen or nitrogen.
4


Homochirality
The use of only one enantiomer of each kind of building block, as in living organisms.
11


Hybrid orbital
A combination of s and p orbitals pointing in the direction of a bond; sp3, sp2 and sp hybrids correspond to tetrahedral, planar and linear geometry.
3


Hydration shell
The layer of oriented water molecules surrounding a dissolved ion or polar molecule.
5


Hydrocarbon
A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
11


Hydrogen bond
An attraction X–H···Y between a hydrogen atom bonded to an electronegative atom X (usually O or N) and an atom Y carrying a lone pair (usually O or N).
5


Hydrogen-bond acceptor
The atom with a lone pair, usually O or N, that receives a hydrogen bond.
5


Hydrogen-bond donor
The group X–H, usually O–H or N–H, that provides the hydrogen atom of a hydrogen bond.
5


Hydrolysis
A reaction in which water breaks a bond, its H going to one fragment and its OH to the other; the reverse of condensation.
7


Hydronium ion
The ion H3O+, a water molecule carrying an extra proton.
7


Hydrophilic
Interacting favourably with water; describing polar and charged groups.
5


Hydrophobic
Not interacting favourably with water; describing non-polar groups.
5


Hydrophobic effect
The tendency of non-polar molecules to cluster together in water, reducing their contact with it.
5


Hydroxide ion
The ion OH−.
7


Hydroxy group
The group –OH bonded to a carbon atom.
4


Ideal gas law
The relation pV = nRT between the pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature of a gas.
6


Independent events
Events such that the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other; the probability that all occur is the product of their probabilities.
1


Intermolecular force
An attraction between molecules, much weaker than a covalent bond.
5


International System of Units (SI)
The system of units used in science, built on seven base units including the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.
1


Ion
An atom or group of atoms that carries a net electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
2


Ion product of water (Kw)
The equilibrium constant for the self-ionisation of water, 1.0 × 10−14 at 25 °C (pKw = 13.99).
8


Ionic bond
The electrical attraction between oppositely charged ions.
3


Ionic compound
A compound made of positive and negative ions held together by their electrical attraction, forming a crystal rather than separate molecules.
2


Ionisation energy (first)
The minimum energy needed to remove one electron from a neutral atom in its ground state.
3


Isomers
Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structures.
4


Isotope
One of two or more forms of an element whose atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
2


Joule
The SI unit of energy, 1 kg m2 s−2.
9


Kelvin (K)
The SI unit of absolute temperature; T/K = t/°C + 273.15.
1


Ketone
A compound in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms.
11


Ketose
A sugar whose carbonyl group is a ketone.
11


Kinetic control
A situation in which the products are determined by the relative rates of competing reactions.
10


Le Chatelier’s principle
The rule that a system at equilibrium, when disturbed, shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance.
8


Leaving group
The group that departs, with its bonding electrons, when a nucleophile attacks an atom.
11


Lewis structure
A drawing of a molecule in which shared electron pairs are shown as lines and lone pairs as pairs of dots.
3


Limiting reactant
The reactant that is used up first in a reaction and so determines the amount of product formed.
7


Liquid
A state of matter in which particles are close together but can move past one another, so that the substance takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume.
2


Logarithm (log10)
The power to which 10 must be raised to give a number: log10 1000 = 3.
1


Logarithmic axis
A graph axis on which equal distances represent equal factors, so that 1, 10, 100 and 1000 are equally spaced.
1


Logarithmic scale
A scale that reports a quantity by its logarithm, so that each step of 1 is a factor of ten; examples are pH and log epsilon.
1


Lone pair
A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond.
3


Mass number (A)
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
2


Mechanism
The step-by-step description of how a reaction occurs.
11


Metal
An element that conducts electricity and heat, has a lustre, and in compounds tends to lose electrons and form cations.
2


Methyl group
The group CH3–.
4


Mixture
A sample of matter containing two or more pure substances in proportions that can vary.
2


Molar (M)
The unit mol L−1 of amount concentration.
6


Molar gas constant (R)
The constant in the ideal gas law, 8.314 J mol−1 K−1; the product of the Avogadro and Boltzmann constants.
6


Molar mass (M)
The mass of one mole of a substance, usually in g mol−1; numerically equal to the relative molecular mass.
6


Mole (mol)
The SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 × 1023 specified entities.
6


Molecular formula
A formula that gives only the number of atoms of each element in a molecule, such as C2H6O.
4


Molecule
A group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds; the smallest unit of a molecular substance.
2


Monomer
A small molecule that can be joined with others of its kind to form a polymer.
12


Natural logarithm (ln)
The logarithm to base e; ln x = 2.303 log10 x.
1


Neutral
Describing a solution in which the concentrations of H3O+ and OH− are equal; pH 7.00 at 25 °C.
8


Neutron
An uncharged particle in the nucleus, with a mass of 1.6749 × 10−27 kg.
2


Nitrile
A compound containing a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen, –C\(\equiv\)N.
11


Noble gas
An element of group 18 (helium, neon, argon and heavier), with a filled outer shell; noble gases hardly react.
2


Non-metal
An element that does not have metallic properties and in compounds tends to gain or share electrons; examples are H, C, N, O, P, S and Cl.
2


Nucleobase
A flat, nitrogen-containing ring compound (A, G, C, U or T) that is part of a nucleotide.
12


Nucleon
A proton or a neutron.
2


Nucleophile
An electron-rich species that forms a bond by donating an electron pair.
11


Nucleoside
A nucleobase bonded to carbon 1\('\) of a sugar.
12


Nucleotide
A nucleoside carrying one or more phosphate groups, usually on carbon 5\('\).
12


Nucleus
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
2


Octet rule
The tendency of atoms to form bonds until they are surrounded by eight valence electrons, the arrangement of a noble gas.
3


Oligomer
A short chain of a few monomer units.
12


Orbital
The region around a nucleus in which an electron of a given energy is likely to be found.
3


Order of magnitude
The power of ten nearest to a quantity; quantities that differ by a factor of about ten differ by one order of magnitude.
1


Order of reaction
The sum of the powers of the concentrations in the rate law.
10


Organic compound
A compound built on a framework of carbon atoms, usually bonded to hydrogen.
3


Oxidation
The loss of electrons, or an increase in oxidation number.
7


Oxidation number
The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were fully ionic, with shared electrons assigned to the more electronegative atom; also called oxidation state.
7


Oxidising agent
A substance that gains electrons and so oxidises another substance.
7


Partial pressure
The pressure that one gas in a mixture would exert if it alone occupied the volume; the partial pressures add up to the total pressure.
6


Pauli exclusion principle
The rule that no two electrons in an atom can be in the same state, so that an orbital holds at most two electrons, of opposite spin.
3


Peptide
A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
12


Peptide bond
The amide bond joining two amino acids in a peptide or protein.
12


Period (periodic table)
A row of the periodic table.
2


Periodic table
An arrangement of the elements in order of atomic number, in rows and columns such that elements with similar chemistry fall in the same column.
2


pH
Minus the logarithm to base 10 of the activity of hydronium ions; each unit is a factor of ten.
8


Phosphate
The polyatomic anion PO43−, a phosphorus atom bonded to four oxygen atoms; also the corresponding group in compounds such as RNA.
2


Phosphate ester
